Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/explore.html

Explore

## Ask anything about a function

Type a formula, or a piecewise function such as `x - n if n:x:!n+1`. Names other than `x` become sliders in steps of 1/8. Choose which questions to ask. Each answer shows its float preview at once and its certified form when it arrives. Your last function is remembered in this browser.

zeros, fmaxima and minimainflection pointspolesopen: undecided, a hole, or a one-sided limit

### Try it

```js
// Everything the explorer does is a few calls.
const f = fn("sin(x)/x");
PRINT("f(1/2) =", f.value("1/2", { digits: 25 }).exact());
PRINT("range on [1, 10]:", f.range(R`1:10`, { digits: 4 }).exact());
PRINT("zeros on [1, 10]:", zeros(f, [1, 10]).exact().length);
PRINT("poles on [-1, 1]:", poles(f, [-1, 1]).exact());
f.integral(1, 10, { digits: 8 }).exact()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/fast.html

Idea

## Fast, then certified

Certified answers cost more than floating-point ones, sometimes a thousand times more. Someone dragging a slider needs a picture now; someone writing down a result needs it to be true. So every question returns a `Refinement` that can answer both ways. It is the same class the RatMath linear algebra and graphics libraries use, so one loop can drive all three.

```js
const job = fn("exp(sin(3x))*x").range(R`0:3`, { digits: 6 });
job.quick;            // { stage: "float", value: [lo, hi], trust: "rough" }
for (const s of job.stages()) …   // float, then progress ticks, then the certified stage
job.exact();          // run to the end now (fine in a Worker)
await job.settle({ signal, sliceMs: 8, onProgress });   // the same, in time slices
```

### A worked run

The range above, run through `stages()` by hand, yields 21 stages:

| stage | what it holds |

| float | [0, 7.1735…] from 256 samples, trust rough. The upper end is a sampled value, so the true maximum may be a little higher. |

| progress 1 of 256 | partial: a certified range from one Taylor model on all of [0, 3], from about −1.5·10⁹ to 1.5·10⁹. Valid, and useless. |

| progress 2 … 19 | partial: the outer bound tightens as the pieces holding the extremes are split; by the second tick it is already about [−186, 196] |

| exact | an interval from just below 0 to 7.17352…, via "Taylor models (order 8) on 25 pieces" |

Every partial is a true enclosure, so a display may show it as soon as it arrives. `of` is the budget (maxPieces), not a forecast: this run stopped after 19 of 256 because outer and inner bounds met.

### What each question previews

| question | preview | trust |

| f.value(x) | the float formula at x | good, or unsure if not finite |

| f.range(I) | min and max of 256 samples | rough |

| f.integral(a, b) | 16-panel Gauss–Legendre | good (rough for piecewise) |

| zeros, extrema, inflections | { kind: "guess", at } from sign changes of f, f′ or f″ on samples | rough |

| p.breaks | none | unsure |

| ode.solve | RK4 samples { t, y } on 200 steps | good, or unsure if it blows up |

### How far to trust a preview

`trust` is `good` when the float computation is normally accurate (a value, an integral by Gauss–Legendre), `rough` when it can miss things (a range from samples can miss a narrow peak; zero guesses come from sign changes, so a double root is invisible), and `unsure` when the float answer is not finite.

### Progress and partial answers

Progress ticks look like `{ stage: "progress", done, of, step, partial }`. `partial` is the answer so far: a range that is already valid but still wide, an integral over the pieces done, the ODE steps validated so far, the zeros found so far. A display can sharpen as they arrive.

### Sliders: live

```js
const f = fn("a*sin(x)", { params: { a: 1 } });
const update = live((a) => f.with({ a }).value("1/2"), (stage) => show(stage.value, stage.exact), { idleMs: 30 });
slider.oninput = () => update(`${slider.value}/8`);
```

Each update shows the preview at once. Certified work starts once the input has been still for `idleMs`, runs in slices, and is cancelled by the next update, so only the latest question is ever finished.

### Your own refinement

A `Refinement` is two functions: one that returns the preview, and a generator that yields progress and returns the certified answer. Anything built this way gets `stages`, `exact`, `settle` and `live` for free.

```js
import { Refinement, fn } from "@ratmath/analytic";

const f = fn("exp(-x^2)");
const area = new Refinement(
  () => ({ value: 0.8820813907, trust: "good" }),   // erf(2)·√π/2 from a table
  function* () {
    const parts = [];
    for (let k = 0; k  a.add(b)), via: "four certified integrals" };
  },
);
const total = await area.settle({ onProgress: (p) => console.log(p.done, "/", p.of) });
```

Cancelling is cooperative: `settle` checks the signal between slices, so a generator that yields often stops quickly. A generator that never yields runs to the end in one slice.

### Try it

```js
const job = fn("exp(sin(3x))*x").range(R`0:3`, { digits: 6 });
PRINT("quick:", job.quick);
for (const s of job.stages()) {
  if (s.stage === "progress") continue;      // there are many progress ticks
  PRINT(s.stage, s.value, s.via ?? "");
}
// settle() is the same work in time slices, so a page stays responsive:
await fn("x*cos(x)").integral(0, 3, { digits: 12 }).settle({ sliceMs: 8 })
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/models.html

Idea

## Taylor models

A Taylor model on a domain D = [a, b] with centre c is a pair (P, I): a polynomial P with exact rational coefficients and a rational interval I, such that

f(x)−P(x−c)∈Ifor every x∈D.
This is the basic object of validated numerics (Berz and Makino's Taylor models, building on Moore's interval analysis). It says more than a value does: it describes f on the whole domain, so ranges, integrals and compositions all come from it with the error already counted. Everything certified in this library is built from it.

### A small example by hand

Take f(x) = eˣ on D = [0, 1/2] with centre c = 1/4 and order 2. Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder says

ex=ec(1+t+2t2​)+eξ6t3​,t=x−c,  ξ between c and x.
Here |t| ≤ 1/4, and e^ξ ≤ e^(1/2) < 1.65, so the last term lies in [−0.0043, 0.0043]. The coefficient e^c is irrational, so the library encloses it, puts the midpoint of each coefficient into P, and adds the leftover radius times the range of its power of t to I. The result is a polynomial with exact rational coefficients and a remainder interval that together contain eˣ for every x in D.

### Arithmetic on models

- Sums add the polynomials and add the remainders.

- Products multiply the polynomials exactly, keep the terms up to the order, and move the rest into the remainder: the dropped high-degree part (bounded over D), plus P·J + Q·I + I·J for (P, I)·(Q, J).

- Division is multiplication by the reciprocal model, which needs the divisor's range to exclude 0.

- Constants may be intervals, so a parameter known only to lie in [1, 2] is a model with P = 3/2 and I = [−1/2, 1/2].

Each bound in these steps is a range of an exact polynomial, so nothing is lost except what is deliberately moved into the remainder.

### Elementary functions of a model

To apply exp, sin, log and the others to a model g, the library uses the outer function's own Taylor series about c₀ = g(c), the value at the centre, and substitutes the model of g − c₀. The Lagrange remainder f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n+1)!·(g − c₀)ⁿ⁺¹ needs a bound on f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ over the whole range of g:

| f | bound on f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ used | condition |

| exp | e^(max of g) | max of g below 2¹⁶ |

| sin, cos | 1 | none |

| log, 1/x | n!/\|g\|ⁿ⁺¹ at the end nearest 0 | range of g excludes 0 (log: above 0) |

| sqrt | from the binomial series | range of g above 0 |

| atan | (k − 1)!/(1 + g²)^(k/2) | none |

When the condition fails, the library refuses with a reason. Coefficients that are irrational, like e^c, are certified intervals; their midpoints go into P and their radii into I.

```js
import { TM, Domain, exp, sin } from "@ratmath/analytic";
import { R } from "@ratmath/core";

const D = Domain(R`0:1/2`);          // centre defaults to the midpoint, 1/4
const x = TM.x(D, { order: 12 });    // the identity model
const g = exp(sin(x)).multiply(x);
g.coefficients;   // exact Rationals, in powers of (x − 1/4)
g.remainder;      // a tiny RationalInterval
g.at(R`1/5`);     // enclosure of g(1/5)
g.range();        // Bernstein bounds with bisection
g.integral();     // certified ∫ over D
g.describe();     // domain, order, remainder width, rules used
```

### How fast the remainder shrinks

For a function that is analytic on a neighbourhood of D, the remainder of an order-n model behaves like (h/2)ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)!·max|f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾|, where h is the width of D. Two levers make it small: a higher order, or a narrower domain. Higher orders pay off until n passes the size of f's derivatives; after that each extra order buys a roughly fixed number of digits. Narrower domains pay off for any function, which is why ranges and integrals split into pieces.

Order costs time too: a product of two order-n models is an O(n²) polynomial product with exact rationals, and each elementary function needs n + 1 of them. The defaults (order 12, 96 bits for irrational constants) are a balance for interactive use.

### Derivatives

The remainder of a model says nothing about the derivative's error: f could wiggle inside the band P ± I with any slope. So `model.derivative()` only works for exact polynomials, and derivatives are taken from the formula instead ([symbolic d/dx](https://ratmath.com/analytic/expressions.html)), then modelled afresh with their own remainder.

### Try it

```js
const D = Domain(R`0:1/2`);             // centre: the midpoint, 1/4
const x = TM.x(D, { order: 12 });       // the identity model on D
const g = exp(sin(x)).multiply(x);
PRINT("first coefficients:", g.coefficients.slice(0, 4));
PRINT("remainder:", g.remainder);
PRINT("g(1/5) is in", g.at(R`1/5`));
PRINT("range:", g.range());
PRINT("integral over D:", g.integral());
g.describe()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/values.html

Topic

## Values to many digits

Ask for f(x) at a rational x and you get two answers. The first is a double-precision float, computed at once. The second is a rational interval that provably contains the true value, narrowed until it is good to the number of significant digits you asked for. This page is about the second one: how a finite computation can promise something about e^(1/3), which no finite decimal equals.

### Reading the answer

Results are shown in RatMath's interval notation. `0.46235716975[69:70]` means the value lies between 0.4623571697569 and 0.4623571697570: the digits outside the brackets are shared by both ends, and the bracket gives the last digits of each end. When the two ends are equal the value is exact, and only one number is shown.

"Digits" means significant digits relative to max(1, |value|). So 20 digits of e^30 ≈ 1.07·10¹³ is an interval about 10⁻⁷ wide, while 20 digits of sin(10⁻⁵) is an interval about 10⁻²⁰ wide. Values near 0 are measured against 1, because "20 significant digits of a number that might be 0" has no finite answer.

```js
import { fn } from "@ratmath/analytic";

const v = fn("exp(x)").value("1/3", { digits: 50 });
v.quick.value;     // 1.3956124250860895 (a double, right away)
v.exact();         // RationalInterval, width ≤ 10^-50 · 1.39…
v.exactStage().via // "certified enclosure at 191 bits"

fn("x^2 + 1/x").value("3/7").exact();   // 370/147 exactly: no irrational step
```

### Series with a tail you can bound

Every elementary function is computed at a point by summing a power series and adding an explicit bound for the part that was not summed. A series alone is not enough: e^x = Σ xᵏ/k! converges for every x, but at x = 100 its largest term is about 10⁴², so the sum would need hundreds of digits of cancellation. The trick in each case is to move the argument to where the series converges fast, sum there, and move back with an operation whose effect on the error is known.

| Function | Reduction | Series and tail bound |

| exp | r = x / 2ˢ with s chosen so \|r\| 4, subtract 2πk with π certified to extra bits; π's uncertainty times k becomes extra width (both are 1-Lipschitz) | alternating series; once the terms shrink, the tail is at most the last term. Summed in fixed-point integers with outward rounding |

| atan | for x > 2, atan x = π/2 − atan(1/x); for 1/2

### Precision bookkeeping

Each step that can lose accuracy is paid for in advance with extra bits. Squaring doubles a relative error, so s squarings in the exp reduction cost s bits; the series is summed with that many more. Terms are rounded to dyadic rationals (a whole number over a power of 2) so their denominators stay small, and every rounding adds one unit in the last place to a running error term that becomes part of the interval. Nothing is estimated: the width of the answer is an upper bound built from the tail bound, the rounding count and the reduction error.

If the first precision is not enough (a value close to a large cancellation, or a composite like exp(sin(x)) whose inner error grows through the outer function), the certified stage doubles the working bits and tries again, up to `maxBits` (default 8192). Each try is a progress tick with a partial interval, so a page can show the answer sharpening.

### Composite formulas

A formula like `exp(sin(x))·x` is evaluated as a Taylor model of order 0 on the point domain {x}: each function receives an interval and returns an interval. At a point that is ordinary interval arithmetic with the certified point values above. The answer is good to the digits asked for when the final width says so, not because each step was given a fixed number of digits.

```js
import { enclose, constants } from "@ratmath/analytic";
import { R } from "@ratmath/core";

enclose.exp(R`1/3`, 200);   // an Iv with relative width about 2^-200
constants.pi(256);          // π to 256 bits
constants.e(128);
```

### Try it

```js
const v = fn("exp(x)").value("1/3", { digits: 50 });
PRINT("quick:", v.quick.value);
PRINT("certified:", v.exact());
PRINT("how:", v.exactStage().via);
PRINT("rational formula, exact:", fn("x^2 + 1/x").value("3/7").exact());
PRINT("π to 128 bits:", constants.pi(128));
enclose.exp(R`1/3`, 100)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/expressions.html

Topic

## Formulas and derivatives

Everything in the library that works with "a function" starts from a formula in calculator notation. `fn(text)` parses it into a small tree, and every question (a value, a range, an integral, zeros, a derivative) is answered by walking that tree in one of three ways.

### The notation

| Write | Means |

| + − * / | the usual operations, left to right at equal precedence: x/2y is (x/2)·y |

| ^ or ** | powers; -x^2 is −(x²) |

| 2x, 2(x+1), x sin(x) | implicit multiplication |

| sin x | a function applied to the next factor, the same as sin(x) |

| sin cos tan asin acos atan exp log ln log1p sqrt cbrt sinh cosh tanh erf | the elementary functions (log and ln are both natural log) |

| abs min max | non-smooth functions, modelled where they are smooth (see below) |

| pi e | constants, certified to the working precision |

| 1/3, 0.25, 2.5E-3 | exact rationals: 0.25 is 1/4, not a double |

### Three ways to walk the tree

- Floats. compileFloat turns the tree into a JavaScript closure on doubles. This drives every preview, plot and slider: thousands of evaluations a frame.

- Taylor models. modelOf evaluates the tree with Taylor models in place of numbers, which gives polynomial-plus-remainder enclosures on a whole interval. Ranges, integrals and many-digit values use this.

- Plain intervals. encloseAst evaluates with intervals. It is cruder but cheap, and the zero finder uses it thousands of times to throw away pieces where f cannot vanish.

The tree is shared with `@ratmath/graphics`, so the formula a plot draws is literally the formula the proofs are about.

### Symbolic d/dx

Derivatives are taken on the tree with the rules from a first calculus course, and the result is a new formula:

| Rule | d/dx |

| sum, product | u′ + v′, u′v + uv′ |

| quotient | (u′v − uv′)/v² |

| constant power | n·uⁿ⁻¹·u′ |

| general power | uᵛ·(v′·ln u + v·u′/u) |

| chain | sin u → cos u·u′, exp u → exp u·u′, log u → u′/u, atan u → u′/(1 + u²), sqrt u → u′/(2·sqrt u), … |

The builders simplify as they go: constants fold, 0·u and 1·u disappear, u − (−v) becomes u + v, and (uᵐ)ⁿ becomes uᵐⁿ. That keeps derivative trees small enough to evaluate quickly, which matters because the zero finder needs f′, f″ and sometimes f‴. Shared subtrees (sin(u) → cos(u)·u′ keeps the same u) are evaluated once.

```js
fn("x^3 + 2x - 1/x").derivative().toString();   // "3*x^2 + 2 + 1/x^2"
format(differentiate(parse("atan(x^2)"), "x"));  // "2*x/(1 + x^4)"
format(differentiate(parse("sin(x)/x"), "x"));   // "(cos(x)*x - sin(x))/x^2"
```

Why not differentiate a Taylor model instead? Because the remainder only bounds f − P, not f′ − P′: f could wiggle inside the remainder band with any slope. The derivative is a new formula, modelled afresh with its own proven remainder.

### Parameters, sliders and intervals

Names other than the variable are parameters. They must be given values, and `with` makes a copy with new values, which is what a slider does:

```js
const f = fn("a*x^2 + b", { params: { a: "3/8", b: 1 } });
f.with({ a: 2 }).value(3).exact();      // 19, exactly
fn("y*t", { variable: "t", params: { y: 2 } });   // a different variable name
```

A parameter can also be an interval. Then every answer holds for every value of the parameter in that interval at once: the range below is a range over both x and a. This is how uncertainty in a measured constant carries through to a proven conclusion. The answer cannot be sharper than the parameter allows: here the range search stops at its piece budget, and the outer bound it reports is still a valid range for all a at once.

### Non-smooth pieces

`abs`, `min` and `max` have no Taylor series at their corners. They are modelled exactly where they are smooth on the domain (the argument of abs keeps one sign, or one argument of min stays below the other) and refused where they are not, with a reason. Split the domain at the corner, or write the function [piecewise](https://ratmath.com/analytic/piecewise.html), where each piece is smooth by construction.

### Refusals

A formula that cannot be bounded on the domain is refused with an `AnalyticError` that has a `code` and a reason: `log` of a range that reaches 0, a divisor whose range contains 0, `sqrt` of something that may be negative, `exp` of something above 2¹⁶. The library never returns a bound it has not proven.

### Try it

```js
PRINT(fn("x^3 + 2x - 1/x").derivative().toString());
PRINT(format(differentiate(parse("atan(x^2)"), "x")));
PRINT(format(differentiate(parse("sin(x)/x"), "x")));

const f = fn("a*x^2 + b", { params: { a: "3/8", b: 1 } });
PRINT("with a = 2, f(3) =", f.with({ a: 2 }).value(3).exact());
fn("y*t", { variable: "t", params: { y: 2 } }).value(5).exact()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/ranges.html

Topic

## Ranges and integrals

The range of f on [a, b] is the interval from its smallest to its largest value there. Sampling finds values inside the range, but it can miss a narrow peak between samples, so a sampled range is only ever a lower estimate of the true one. A certified range is an interval that provably contains every value, and that is tight enough to be useful.

### The dependency problem

The simplest certified method is interval arithmetic: replace x by the interval [a, b] and compute. Every operation's result contains all possible results, so the answer is valid. But it forgets that the two x's in a formula are the same number. On [0, 1], x·(1 − x) becomes [0, 1]·[0, 1] = [0, 1], while the true range is [0, 1/4]. And x − x becomes [−1, 1] instead of 0. The overestimate shrinks only in proportion to the width of the interval.

Taylor models fix most of this. They keep the dependence on x as a polynomial with exact coefficients, so x − x is exactly the zero polynomial and x·(1 − x) is exactly x − x². What is left is to bound a polynomial, and that has a good answer.

### Bounding a polynomial: the Bernstein form

Rewrite P on [a, b] in the Bernstein basis: with t = (x − a)/(b − a),

P(x)=k=0∑n​βk​(kn​)tk(1−t)n−k.
The basis functions are nonnegative and add up to 1, so P(x) is a weighted average of the coefficients βₖ: its range lies between min βₖ and max βₖ. The end coefficients are exact values, β₀ = P(a) and βₙ = P(b). The coefficients come from the power-basis ones by an exact rational transformation, and when the interval is halved (de Casteljau's algorithm), the gap between the Bernstein bound and the true range shrinks like the square of the width. The library bisects a few times by default.

A Taylor model's range is then that polynomial bound plus the remainder interval.

### Adaptive pieces

`f.range(I)` keeps a list of pieces, each with its own Taylor model. Two bounds are tracked:

- the outer bound: the hull of every piece's model bound. The true range is inside it.

- the inner bound: from certified values at piece midpoints. The true maximum is at least the largest of them, and the true minimum at most the smallest.

Only the pieces that hold the current outer extremes are split, so the work goes to where the maximum and minimum are, and the search stops when outer and inner bounds agree to the requested digits. The answer is the outer bound, so it is a true enclosure whose excess is at most that tolerance.

```js
const r = fn("x*cos(x)").range(R`0:3`, { digits: 6 });
r.quick.value;   // [lo, hi] from 256 samples, marked "rough"
r.exact();       // RationalInterval containing every value of x·cos(x) on [0, 3]
r.exactStage().via   // "Taylor models (order 8) on 28 pieces"
```

### Integrals

A Taylor model integrates exactly: if f(x) − P(x − c) ∈ I on [a, b], then

∫ab​f∈∫ab​P(x−c)dx+I⋅(b−a),
and the integral of P is an exact rational. The width of the answer is the width of I times the length of the interval. `f.integral(a, b)` splits [a, b] into pieces until each piece's width is at most its share of the tolerance (in proportion to its length), so the effort goes to the parts where f is hard to approximate. The preview is a 16-panel Gauss–Legendre sum on doubles.

The number of pieces grows slowly with the digits asked for. An order-n model on a piece of width h has a remainder of order hⁿ⁺¹, so halving every piece gains about n + 1 bits, or around 4 digits at order 12, while doubling the work.

### Integrable singularities and holes

A removable gap in a rational part, as in (x² − 1)/(x − 1) + sin(2x)/2, is cancelled exactly before integrating, so the integral across x = 1 works. A true singularity, such as 1/√x at 0, makes the models' remainders unbounded and the integral is refused rather than guessed.

### Try it

```js
const r = fn("x*cos(x)").range(R`0:3`, { digits: 6 });
PRINT("quick (sampled):", r.quick.value, r.quick.trust);
PRINT("certified:", r.exact());
PRINT("how:", r.exactStage().via);
const I = fn("exp(-x^2)").integral(0, 2, { digits: 12 });
PRINT("∫₀² exp(−x²):", I.exact());
I.exactStage().via
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/zeros.html

Topic

## Zeros, poles and extrema

Finding where f = 0 numerically is easy. Proving it is harder: that there is a zero in a bracket, that there is only one, and that there are none elsewhere. The library uses two engines.

### Rational functions: exact

When f is built from + − × ÷ and integer powers with rational numbers, it is read exactly as N/D. Then:

- Holes. G = gcd(N, D) cancels. Points where G = 0 are holes: f is undefined there, but the limit exists, and the library reports it.

- Multiplicity. Yun's square-free decomposition writes N/G = a₁·a₂²·a₃³⋯ with each aᵢ free of repeated roots, so every root comes with its multiplicity, and every pole with its order.

- Isolation. A Sturm sequence counts the distinct roots in any interval exactly. Bisection splits at the simplest rational in the middle half of each bracket, so roots like 1 or −2/3 are hit exactly, and irrational roots end in brackets like [1393/985, 1970/1393] around √2.

### Everything else: Krawczyk

For a bracket X with midpoint m, Y ≈ 1/f′(m), and an interval bound F′(X) on the derivative,

K=m−Yf(m)+(1−YF′(X))(X−m)
contains every zero of f in X. If K misses X, there is no zero. If K lies inside X, there is exactly one, and replacing X by K ∩ X narrows it quadratically, like Newton's method but with proof. Where F′(X) contains 0 (a double root, two close roots), the test cannot decide, so the bracket is reported as `possible`, with `atMost: m` when the m-th derivative is proven nonzero there: by Rolle's theorem, f then has at most m zeros there, counted with multiplicity.

At an exact zero, the derivatives that are exactly 0 there give a lower bound on the multiplicity. When Rolle's bound matches it nearby, the multiplicity is proven. So sin(x)² has a zero of multiplicity exactly 2 at 0, while near π it can only say "at most 2": no finite computation can tell a double root from two very close roots, or from a near miss.

### Functions flat to every order

e^(−1/x²) and all its derivatives tend to 0 at x = 0. Near 0 it is smaller than any number the library can represent, so it cannot be told apart from 0 there. Those brackets come back as `possible` with `bound`, the proven maximum of |f| on them, and with no `atMost`, because every derivative is just as flat. Outside them f is proven positive.

### Poles, extrema, inflections

Poles are zeros of denominators (and of cos inside tan) where the numerator is proven nonzero, and only where the blow-up reaches f. A division inside exp is not a pole of f: e^(−1/x²) tends to 0. Extrema are zeros of f′, classified by the sign of f″ or by the sign change of f′. Inflection points are zeros of f″ where f″ changes sign.

When f′ has the same proven sign at both ends of an undecided bracket, the record carries `touching: true`. Then either f′ only touches 0 there and f has no extremum (1 + cos 2x at π/2 is like this), or a maximum and a minimum sit together inside the bracket. No finite precision can tell these apart when the touch is at an irrational point, so this is the strongest honest answer.

### Holes and removable points

Some formulas are undefined at a point where the function has an obvious value. The library handles two common kinds exactly.

- Rational parts. In (x² − 1)/(x − 1) + sin(2x)/2, the summands that are rational functions of x are combined into N/D and the exact gcd is cancelled. Questions are then answered for x + 1 + sin(2x)/2, and x = 1 is reported as a hole with the limit as its value.

- Quotients with a polynomial denominator. For sin(x)/x (also 4·sin(x)/x or sin(x)/x + x, which are rewritten as one quotient), the denominator's exact zero c = 0 is a hole when the numerator vanishes there to the same order k. L'Hôpital's rule gives the limit u⁽ᵏ⁾(c)/v⁽ᵏ⁾(c), exactly 1 here. Near c, the m-th derivative is written as Nₘ/v^(m+1) and enclosed with the mean-value form of Taylor's theorem, so the searches for extrema and inflections pass straight through the hole.

Results exactly at a hole are dropped from zeros, extrema and inflections, because f itself is not defined there; `poles` lists the hole with its value, so a plot can draw an open dot.

```js
poles("sin(x)/x", [-4, 4]).exact();    // [{ kind: "hole", at: 0, value: [1, 1] }]
extrema("sin(x)/x", [-8, 8]).exact();  // min, min at ±4.4934 and max, max at ±7.7253
```

### Logs and square roots

ln(g) tends to −∞ where g tends to 0 from above, so `poles` reports a zero of g as `kind: "pole"` with `source: "log"`, again only where the blow-up reaches f: x·ln(x) has none, since it tends to 0. Zeros of sqrt(g), gᵖ (p > 0), abs(g) and constant multiples are found as zeros of g, which avoids the infinite slope of the square root at its zeros. Through an even power, sqrt or abs, f does not change sign at the zero, so a proven single zero inside a bracket is reported as `isolated` rather than `sign-change`.

### Budgets

The general engine works through a stack of brackets and pauses every 15 ms, so a page that calls `settle()` stays responsive. Each starting piece has a budget (`maxBoxes`, default 2000, and a share of `maxMs`, default 8000). Brackets left when it runs out come back as `possible`, and the `via` line says the budget was hit.

### Try it

```js
PRINT("poles of sin(x)/x:", poles("sin(x)/x", [-4, 4]).exact());
for (const e of extrema("sin(x)/x", [-8, 8]).exact()) PRINT(e.kind, "near", e.lo.toDecimal(5), e.unique ? "(unique)" : "");
const z = zeros("x^3 - 2", [0, 2]).exact();
PRINT("cube root of 2 lies in", z[0].lo, "to", z[0].hi);
inflections("x^3 - 3x", [-2, 2]).exact()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/piecewise.html

Topic

## Piecewise functions

A piecewise function is a list of pairs: a region and a rule. The first region that contains x decides the rule. Regions use a betweenness chain on x:

| region | meaning |

| 2:x:8 | 2 ≤ x ≤ 8 |

| _:x:8 2:x:_ | x ≤ 8 x ≥ 2 (_ is an unbounded side) |

| 2:!x:8 2:x:!8 | 2 1 |

| all, else, otherwise | every x |

A name in a bound that is not a parameter is an integer variable. Bounds must be affine in it (like 2n + 1 or 3 − n/2). For each x the library solves for the integer n that fits, and the rule can use n too: `x - n if n:x:!n+1` is the sawtooth. A region can also be a plain function `x => boolean`; it answers point questions, but ranges, integrals and zeros need breakpoints, which only chains provide.

```js
fn("x^2 if _:x:1; 3 - x if 1:!x:2; 1/2 otherwise");
piecewise([["2n:x:!2n+1", "1"], ["2n+1:x:!2n+2", "-1"]]);   // a square wave
where`${a}:!x:${b}`;                                          // a Region from a template
```

### Breaks

`breaks([a, b])` lists each breakpoint with the value there (if any piece contains it), the limits from the left and right rules, and a kind. `continuous` means all three are proven equal. `jump` means the two limits are proven different. `removable` means the limits agree but the value is missing or different. That is what a plot needs to draw filled and open dots.

### Worked example: breaks

```js
const f = fn("x^2 if _:x:1; 3 - x if 1:!x:2; 1/2 otherwise");
f.breaks([-1, 3]).exact();
```

| at | value | left | right | kind |

| 1 | 1 (from x², since _:x:1 is closed) | 1 | 2 | jump |

| 2 | 1 (from 3 − x, since 1:!x:2 is closed at 2) | 1 | 1/2 | jump |

Each limit is the rule of the neighbouring piece evaluated at the breakpoint, enclosed as an interval. A jump is proven when the left and right enclosures are disjoint; continuity is proven when all three are exact and equal; `edge` marks a break with a piece on only one side. When the enclosures overlap without being equal (a limit like sin(π)/π that is 0 but is only known to lie in a tiny interval) the kind is `unproven`, never a guess.

### How the integer variable is solved

For a chain such as `2n : x :! 2n+1` the bounds are affine in n, so each inequality is a bound on n: 2n ≤ x gives n ≤ x/2, and x < 2n + 1 gives n > (x − 1)/2. The library takes the floor and ceiling of those rational bounds and checks the integers between them, so it never searches. `breakpoints(a, b)` works the same way in reverse: it lists the integers n whose bounds 2n and 2n + 1 fall in [a, b], which is how ranges, integrals and zeros know where to split.

Exact answers follow. The sawtooth `x - n if n:x:!n+1` has integral 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/8 = 9/8 from 0 to 5/2, and the library returns the point interval 9/8. The square wave above has integral 1 − 1 + 1 − 1/2 = 1/2 from 0 to 7/2, also exactly.

### Questions piece by piece

Values, ranges, integrals, zeros, extrema and inflections are answered on each open piece with that piece's rule, then combined. A sign change across a jump is not a zero. The zero finder only looks inside pieces and at points where the value is exactly 0.

```js
const g = fn("x^2 - 2 if _:x:!1; x - 1/2 otherwise");
g.zeros([-3, 3]).exact();
// one record: sign-change in [−1970/1393, −1393/985], unique: the zero −√2.
// x − 1/2 is never 0 on x ≥ 1, and the drop from −1 to 1/2 at x = 1 is a jump, not a zero.
```

The range of a piecewise function is the hull of the ranges of its pieces and of the values at its breakpoints. A piece that is open at a breakpoint contributes its limit there to the outer bound, so the range of the sawtooth on [0, 3] comes back as [0, 1]: a true enclosure, even though the value 1 is approached and never taken.

### Try it

```js
const f = fn("x^2 if _:x:1; 3 - x if 1:!x:2; 1/2 otherwise");
for (const x of ["0", "1", "3/2", "5/2"]) PRINT(`f(${x}) =`, f.value(x).exact());
PRINT("breaks:", f.breaks([-1, 3]).exact());
const g = fn("x^2 - 2 if _:x:!1; x - 1/2 otherwise");
PRINT("zeros of g:", g.zeros([-3, 3]).exact());
const wave = piecewise([["2n:x:!2n+1", "1"], ["2n+1:x:!2n+2", "-1"]]);
[0, "1/2", 1, "3/2", "7/2"].map((x) => wave.value(x).exact())
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/odes.html

Topic

## Differential equations

An ordinary differential equation y′ = F(t, y) with a starting value y(t₀) = y₀ usually has no formula for its solution. A numerical method such as Runge–Kutta gives good approximations, but with no statement of how good. A validated solver gives an enclosure: a tube of functions that provably contains the true solution on the whole time span.

### The fixed-point idea

Integrating both sides turns the equation into a fixed-point problem. The solution is the function y with

y=Φ(y),Φ(y)(t)=y0​+∫t0​t​F(s,y(s))ds.
Picard iteration applies Φ repeatedly, starting from the constant y₀. Each application adds one correct Taylor coefficient. That gives the polynomial part of the enclosure. The proof comes from looking for a set that Φ maps into itself.

### One validated step

On a step [t₀, t₀ + h]:

- Iterate Φ on polynomials, n times for order n, to get P ≈ y on the step.

- Guess a remainder interval I and evaluate Φ(P + I) in Taylor-model arithmetic. If the result lies inside P + I, Φ maps the set of functions within I of P into itself. That set is convex and Φ is compact there, so by Schauder's fixed-point theorem it holds a fixed point, which is a solution; for the smooth right-hand sides here the solution is unique, so the true solution stays within I of P on the whole step.

- If the inclusion fails, widen I a few times; if it still fails, halve h and start the step again.

- Once it holds, apply Φ again: the image is a tighter enclosure, often by a lot.

The step ends with an enclosure of y(t₀ + h), which is the starting set for the next step.

```js
import { ode } from "@ratmath/analytic";

const sol = ode.solve({ f: "y^2 + t", y0: "1/2", until: "1/2", order: 10 });
sol.quick.value;       // { t, y }: an RK4 preview on 200 steps
const S = sol.exact(); // an ODESolution
S.final;               // RationalInterval enclosing y(1/2)
S.at("1/4");           // enclosure at any t in the span
S.steps;               // [{ t0, t1, models }]: one Taylor model per step
S.describe();
```

### Step sizes

A long step needs fewer steps but a larger remainder; a short one is tighter but costs more. The solver measures how much width each step adds beyond the width it inherited. It halves h while halving still reduces that excess, doubles h after a success (up to the first step size), and gives up on a span only when h falls below `minStep`. A solution that blows up, such as y′ = y² from y(0) = 1 near t = 1, ends with `complete: false` and a reason, never with a wrong enclosure.

### Uncertain starting values

The starting value can be an interval. Then the enclosure contains every solution that starts in it. For y′ = y the solutions are y₀·eᵗ, so the true set of solutions grows in width by exactly eᵗ. The enclosure grows faster than that, because each step treats its starting interval as a fresh interval and loses the fact that all its points move together. The answer is still a proof; it is just looser than it could be. Keeping the dependence on y₀ as an extra variable of the Taylor models would fix this, and is on the list of things not built yet.

### Systems and the wrapping effect

A system has one equation per component, and the enclosure is a box: one interval per component. Give the right-hand sides as a list and name the variables:

```js
ode.solve({ f: ["v", "-x"], vars: ["x", "v"], y0: [1, 0], until: 3 });     // x″ = −x
ode.solve({ f: ["y2", "-y1 + mu*(1 - y1^2)*y2"], y0: [2, 0], until: 1, params: { mu: 1 } });
```

Boxes have a weakness. A rotating flow turns each box, and the smallest box around a turned box is larger than the box was. Each step inherits that larger box, so over long spans the enclosure grows even when the true set of solutions does not. This is the wrapping effect, first described by Moore. The solver counters it by also following how the solution depends on its starting value (the variational equation) and carrying the uncertainty in coordinates that turn with the flow, so the box is not redrawn at every step. For the oscillator this ends near 10⁻¹⁴ wide at t = 3. Pass `track: false` to switch it off: steps are then 2 to 5 times faster and the box grows as described. `until` may also be less than `t0`, which integrates backward in time.

### Try it

```js
const sol = ode.solve({ f: "y^2 + t", y0: "1/2", until: "1/2", order: 10 });
const S = sol.exact();
PRINT("y(1/2) is in", S.final);
PRINT("y(1/4) is in", S.at("1/4"));
PRINT("steps:", S.steps.length);
// a system: x″ = −x, so x = cos t
const osc = ode.solve({ f: ["v", "-x"], vars: ["x", "v"], y0: [1, 0], until: 1 }).exact();
PRINT("x(1), v(1) =", osc.final, "  cos 1 ≈", Math.cos(1));
S.describe()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/bvp.html

Topic

## Boundary value problems

An initial value problem fixes y and y′ at one end. A boundary value problem fixes one condition at each end of an interval, and asks for the solution in between:

```js
// y″ = −y, y(0) = 0, y(1) = 1
const s = bvp({ f: "-y", interval: [0, 1], left: { y: 0 }, right: { y: 1 } }).exact();
s.start;       // the slope y′(0), enclosed: 1/sin(1)
s.at("1/2");   // y(1/2), enclosed
s.unique;      // true: the equation is linear
```

`f` is the formula for y″ in `x`, `y` and `dy` (rename them with `time` and `vars`). Each condition is `{ y: value }` or `{ dy: value }`.

### Shooting, with proof

One value at the left end is not given: the slope, when y(a) is. Call it s. For each s the initial value problem has a solution, and the right-hand condition is missed by some amount g(s). The preview finds a root of g in Float64, by the secant method on RK4 solves. The exact stage then:

- takes a small bracket [s₋, s₊] around that root;

- solves the initial value problem from s₋ and from s₊ with the validated solver (see Differential equations), and checks that the enclosures of g(s₋) and g(s₊) have opposite signs;

- solves once more from the whole bracket. If that solve reaches b, every solution starting in the bracket exists up to b, so g is continuous on the bracket.

By the intermediate value theorem, g has a root in the bracket: a solution of the boundary value problem exists, its left-end value lies in `start`, and the tube from step 3 encloses it at every x. If a bracket fails, a wider one is tried.

### What is and is not claimed

For a linear equation g is a straight line, so the root is the only one and `unique` is true. For a nonlinear equation there may be other solutions with other slopes; the result is one solution, proven to exist, near the one the preview found. A different `guess` for the unknown value can lead to another. If the Float64 shooting does not converge, there is nothing to certify and the call refuses.

The cost is three validated solves. Linear problems take a fraction of a second. Nonlinear ones are slow over long intervals, because the validated solver is: the pendulum y″ = −sin y on [0, 1] takes about half a minute. Run them in a Worker and show the preview meanwhile.

### Try it

```js
const r = bvp({ f: "y + x", interval: [0, 1], left: { dy: 0 }, right: { y: 1 } });
PRINT("preview of y(0):", r.quick.value.start);
const s = r.exactStage();
PRINT(s.via);
PRINT("y(0) lies in", s.value.start);
PRINT("y(1/2) lies in", s.value.at("1/2"));
s.value.slopeAt(1)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/methods.html

Topic

## First-order equations: the methods

The [validated solver](https://ratmath.com/analytic/odes.html) answers "what is y(2)?" with a proof and no formula. A course asks for the formula and for the method that finds it. `firstOrder` recognises the standard types of equation y′=f(x,y), carries out the method, and reports every step. `exactEquation` does the same for Mdx+Ndy=0.

```js
const s = firstOrder("x - 2*y");          // y' = x - 2y
s.type;       // "linear"
s.general;    // "y = 1/2*x - 1/4 + C*exp(-2*x)"
s.steps;      // [{ what, formula }, …]

const p = s.through(0, 1);                // the solution with y(0) = 1
p.solution;   // "1/2*x - 1/4 + 5/4*exp(-2*x)"
p.check(1);   // { agree: true, numeric: […], formula: […] }
```

### A formula that has been checked

Every closed form here can be compared with the validated numerical solution. `check(x1)` solves the initial value problem to x1​ with proven error bounds and evaluates the formula there with proven error bounds; the two enclosures of y(x1​) must meet. For a solution given only as a relation G(x,y)=C, the relation is evaluated on the numerical enclosure and must contain the constant. A wrong formula fails this test, so a mistake in the algebra cannot pass unnoticed. A check takes from a fraction of a second to some seconds, depending on the equation.

### The types

| type | form | method |

| linear | y′=a(x)+b(x)y | multiply by μ=e−∫bdx; then (μy)′=μa |

| separable | y′=g(x)h(y) | ∫dy/h(y)=∫g(x)dx+C |

| Bernoulli | y′=p(x)y+q(x)yn | v=y1−n makes it linear |

| homogeneous | y′=F(y/x) | y=vx makes it separable: xv′=F(v)−v |

| exact | Mdx+Ndy=0 with My​=Nx​ | find φ with φx​=M, φy​=N; solutions are φ=C |

An equation can be of several types: y′=xy is linear and separable. `types` lists all that apply and `type` is the one used; pass `{ method }` to choose. A linear equation is solved as linear because that gives y outright. A separable equation gives a relation between x and y, reported as `implicit`, and where the relation is easily solved (a logarithm, a reciprocal, an arctangent) also as `general`.

Dividing by h(y) loses the constant solutions y=y0​ with h(y0​)=0. They are listed in `singular`.

### Why the integrating factor works

For y′−by=a, multiply by μ(x). The left side becomes μy′−μby, which is the derivative of the product μy exactly when μ′=−μb, that is μ=e−∫b. Then (μy)′=μa is solved by one integration:

y=μ1​(∫μadx+C).

### Exact equations

If φ(x,y) is constant along a solution then φx​dx+φy​dy=0. So Mdx+Ndy=0 is solved at once if M=φx​ and N=φy​ for some φ, and since mixed partials agree that requires My​=Nx​. When the test fails, a factor μ may repair it: if (My​−Nx​)/N depends on x alone then μ(x)=e∫(My​−Nx​)/Ndx works, and likewise with the roles exchanged. `exactEquation` tries both.

```js
const e = exactEquation("3*x*y + y^2", "x^2 + x*y");
e.exact;       // false
e.factor;      // "x"
e.potential;   // "y*x^3 + 1/2*y^2*x^2"     solutions: that = C
```

### The integrals

The methods need antiderivatives. `antiderivative(tree, name)` covers polynomials, rational functions by partial fractions, exponentials and sines of linear arguments with polynomial factors, and one level of substitution; it returns nothing unless differentiating its answer gives the integrand back. When an integral is not found, `type` is `null` and the validated solver is still there. The fuller engine is in the symbolic package.

| call | returns |

| firstOrder(rhs, { x = "x", y = "y", method }) | { equation, type, types, steps, general, implicit, singular, through } |

| exactEquation(M, N, { x, y }) | the same, with { exact, factor, potential } |

| s.through(x0, y0) | { constant, solution, relation, at(x), check(x1) } |

| antiderivative(tree, name) | { tree, trust: "proven" \| "checked" } or null |

### Try it

```js
// Four equations, four methods; each formula checked against the validated solution.
const show = (s) => {
  PRINT(`${s.equation}    [${s.type}; also fits: ${s.types.filter((t) => t !== s.type).join(", ") || "none"}]`);
  for (const step of s.steps) PRINT(`    ${step.what}:  ${step.formula}`);
};

const linear = firstOrder("x - 2*y");
show(linear);
const p = linear.through(0, 1);
const c = p.check(1);
PRINT(`  through (0, 1): y = ${p.solution}`);
PRINT(`  at x = 1 the formula gives ${c.formula.low.toDecimal(12)}, the validated solver [${c.numeric.low.toDecimal(9)}, ${c.numeric.high.toDecimal(9)}]: agree ${c.agree}`);

const logistic = firstOrder("y*(1 - y)");
show(logistic);
PRINT("  through (0, 1/10): y =", logistic.through(0, "1/10").solution, "  constant solutions:", logistic.singular.join(", "));

show(firstOrder("x*y^2", { method: "separable" }));

const exact = exactEquation("2*x*y + 1", "x^2 + 3*y^2");
show(exact);
exact.through(0, 1).relation;
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/linearodes.html

Topic

## Linear equations and Laplace transforms

`linearODE` solves an​y(n)+⋯+a1​y′+a0​y=g(x) with rational coefficients: the characteristic roots, the solutions of the homogeneous equation, a particular solution by undetermined coefficients or variation of parameters, and the constants from initial values. `laplace` and `inverseLaplace` are the transform route to the same answers.

```js
const s = linearODE([1, -3, 2], "exp(x)");     // y'' - 3y' + 2y = e^x
s.characteristic;   // "r^2 - 3*r + 2 = 0"
s.roots;            // [{ root: "1", … }, { root: "2", … }]
s.basis;            // ["exp(x)", "exp(2*x)"]
s.particular;       // "-(x*exp(x))"      resonance: e^x already solves the homogeneous equation
s.general;          // "y = C1*exp(x) + C2*exp(2*x) - x*exp(x)"

const i = s.initial([1, 0]);                   // y(0) = 1, y'(0) = 0
i.solution;         // "y = -(x*exp(x)) + exp(x)"
i.check(1);         // against the validated numerical solution
```

### The characteristic equation

Trying y=erx in the homogeneous equation gives an​rn+⋯+a0​=0. Each root contributes solutions:

| root | solutions |

| real r, once | erx |

| real r, m times | erx, xerx, …, xm−1erx |

| α±βi | eαxcosβx, eαxsinβx (times powers of x if repeated) |

Roots are found exactly: rational roots with their multiplicities, then quadratic factors, whose roots are written with square roots. A polynomial with an irreducible factor of degree three or more has roots that square roots do not reach, and `linearODE` refuses and points to the numerical solver.

### Undetermined coefficients

When g is a sum of terms xkeaxcoswx or xkeaxsinwx, a particular solution has the same shape with unknown coefficients. If a+wi is a characteristic root s times, the trial solution is multiplied by xs: this is resonance, and it is why y′′+4y=cos2x has the growing solution 41​xsin2x.

The coefficients are found without guessing. On the space spanned by xjeaxcoswx and xjeaxsinwx, differentiation is a matrix, so the whole operator is a matrix, and the coefficients solve a linear system with exact rational arithmetic. `verified` reports that substituting the result back leaves exactly zero.

### Variation of parameters

For other right-hand sides of a second-order equation, with homogeneous solutions y1​,y2​ and Wronskian W=y1​y2′​−y2​y1′​,

yp​=−y1​∫a2​Wy2​g​dx+y2​∫a2​Wy1​g​dx.
It is used when the integrals are found; `method` says which route was taken.

### Laplace transforms

The transform F(s)=∫0∞​e−stf(t)dt turns differentiation into multiplication, L{y′}=sY−y(0), so a linear equation with initial values becomes algebra. The inverse is found by partial fractions.

```js
laplace("t^2*exp(-t)");              // "2/(s + 1)^3"
laplace("t*sin(3*t)");               // "6*s/(s^2 + 9)^2"
laplace("t", { delay: 2 });          // "exp(-2*s)/s^2"   for u(t - 2)·(t - 2)

inverseLaplace("1/(s^2*(s + 1))");
// { partialFractions: "-(1/s) + 1/s^2 + 1/(s + 1)", result: "-1 + t + exp(-t)" }
```

| f(t) | F(s) |

| tkeat | k!/(s−a)k+1 |

| eatcoswt | (s−a)/((s−a)2+w2) |

| eatsinwt | w/((s−a)2+w2) |

| u(t−c)f(t−c) | e−csF(s) |

`laplace` transforms sums of terms tkeatcoswt and tkeatsinwt. `inverseLaplace` inverts rational functions whose denominators split over the rationals into linear factors (to any power) and single quadratic factors. Forcing that switches on at a time, written `heaviside(t - c)`, and impulses, written `dirac(t - c)`, are on the page [Steps and impulses](https://ratmath.com/analytic/switches.html), together with `laplaceSolve`.

| call | returns |

| linearODE(coefficients, forcing = 0, { x, y }) | { characteristic, roots, basis, homogeneous, particular, method, verified, steps, general, initial } |

| s.initial(values, x0 = 0) | { constants, solution, at(x), check(x1) } |

| laplace(f, { t, s, delay }) | a formula in s |

| inverseLaplace(F, { s, t }) | { partialFractions, result } |

| partialFractions(N, D) | { poly, linear, quadratic } for polynomials given as coefficient arrays |

### Try it

```js
// A driven oscillator at resonance: y'' + 4y = cos(2x), starting at rest.
const s = linearODE([1, 0, 4], "cos(2*x)");
for (const step of s.steps) PRINT(`${step.what}:  ${step.formula}`);
PRINT("general:", s.general);
const start = s.initial([0, 0]);
PRINT("from rest:", start.solution);
const c = start.check(3);
PRINT(`y(3): formula ${c.formula.low.toDecimal(10)}, validated solver [${c.numeric.low.toDecimal(8)}, ${c.numeric.high.toDecimal(8)}], agree: ${c.agree}`);

// The same initial value problem by Laplace transform: (s^2 + 4)·Y = s/(s^2 + 4).
PRINT("L{cos 2t} =", laplace("cos(2*t)"));
PRINT("L{t sin 2t / 4} =", laplace("t*sin(2*t)/4"), " which is s/(s^2 + 4)^2, the transform of the solution");

// A damped equation with a repeated root and a polynomial right-hand side.
const d = linearODE([1, 2, 1], "x^2");
PRINT(d.general);
inverseLaplace("(s + 3)/(s^2 + 2*s + 5)").result;
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/switches.html

Topic

## Steps and impulses

Forces that switch on at a time, or strike at an instant, are where the Laplace transform is at its best. A factor `heaviside(t - c)` switches a term on at time c. `dirac(t - c)` is a unit impulse at c. `laplaceSolve` solves a linear equation with such forcing by transform, and then proves the answer piece by piece.

```js
laplace("heaviside(t - 2)");            // "exp(-2*s)/s"
laplace("heaviside(t - 1)*t");          // "exp(-s)*(1/s + 1/s^2)"
laplace("heaviside(t - 1)*sin(t)");     // "exp(-s)*(sin(1)*(s/(s^2 + 1)) + cos(1)*(1/(s^2 + 1)))"
laplace("t*dirac(t - 2)");              // "exp(-2*s)*2"

inverseLaplace("exp(-2*s)/s^2").result;      // "heaviside(t - 2)*(t - 2)"
inverseLaplace("exp(-3*s)").result;          // "dirac(t - 3)"

const r = laplaceSolve([1, 0, 1], "heaviside(t - 1)", [0, 0]);   // y'' + y = u(t − 1), at rest
r.solution;    // "heaviside(t - 1)*(-cos(t - 1) + 1)"
r.pieces;      // [{ from: "0", y: "0" }, { from: "1", y: "-cos(t - 1) + 1" }]
r.verified;    // true
```

### The shift theorems

Write u(t−c) for the unit step that is 0 before c and 1 after, with c≥0. Then

L{u(t−c)g(t)}=e−csL{g(t+c)},L{δ(t−c)g(t)}=e−csg(c).
For the first, substitute τ=t−c in ∫c∞​e−stg(t)dt. For a term g=tkeatcoswt, the shifted g(t+c) is expanded exactly: (t+c)k by the binomial theorem, and cos(wt+wc) by the addition formula. That leaves constants such as eac, coswc and sinwc, which stay as exact formulas. The second is the defining property of the impulse: ∫0∞​e−stδ(t−c)g(t)dt=e−csg(c).

Going back, `inverseLaplace` groups the terms of F(s) by their factor e−cs, inverts each group by partial fractions, and shifts: e−csR(s)↦u(t−c)r(t−c). A constant left over after the partial fractions is an impulse: e−cs↦δ(t−c). A polynomial of higher degree would need derivatives of the impulse, and is refused.

### Solving with switched forcing

For an​y(n)+⋯+a0​y=g(t) with y(0),…,y(n−1)(0) given, transforming gives

p(s)Y(s)=G(s)+j=1∑n​aj​i<j∑​sj−1−iy(i)(0),p(s)=an​sn+⋯+a0​,
and Y=(…)/p(s) is inverted group by group. `steps` records each stage.

```js
const kick = laplaceSolve([1, 2, 5], "dirac(t - 2)", [1, 0]);   // a damped spring, struck at t = 2
kick.solution;
// "cos(2*t)*exp(-t) + 1/2*sin(2*t)*exp(-t) + heaviside(t - 2)*(1/2*sin(2*t - 4)*exp(-t + 2))"

const pulse = laplaceSolve([1, 3, 2], "heaviside(t - 1) - heaviside(t - 3)", [0, 0]);   // on from 1 to 3
pulse.pieces.map((p) => p.from);   // ["0", "1", "3"]
```

### Why the answer is proved, not just computed

Between switching times the forcing is an ordinary formula, and so is the solution. `laplaceSolve` checks, by exact symbolic differentiation:

- On each interval, the piece satisfies the equation identically.

- The first piece has the given initial values.

- At each switching time c, the pieces join with y,y′,…,y(n−2) continuous. At an impulse wδ(t−c), y(n−1) jumps by exactly w/an​; everywhere else it is continuous too.

That is exactly the meaning of a solution with step and impulse forcing. The uniqueness theorem for linear equations then says it is the solution, so `verified: true` is a proof.

| call | returns |

| laplace(f, { t, s, delay }) | a formula in s; f may contain heaviside(t - c) factors and dirac(t - c) |

| inverseLaplace(F, { s, t }) | { partialFractions, result } for sums of e−cs times rational functions |

| laplaceSolve(coefficients, forcing, initial, { t, s }) | { transform, partialFractions, solution, pieces, verified, steps, at(time) } |

`heaviside` and `dirac` are understood by these transform tools only. To evaluate or plot a switched solution, take its pieces.

### Try it

```js
// A spring at rest is pushed by a constant force from t = 1 to t = 3, then struck at t = 5.
const r = laplaceSolve([1, 0, 4], "heaviside(t - 1) - heaviside(t - 3) + dirac(t - 5)", [0, 0]);
for (const step of r.steps) PRINT(`${step.what}${step.value ? ":  " + step.value : ""}`);
for (const p of r.pieces) PRINT(`for t > ${p.from}:  y = ${p.y}`);
PRINT("y(2) =", r.at(2));
// The transform of the pushing force, and back again.
const F = laplace("heaviside(t - 1) - heaviside(t - 3)");
PRINT("L{u(t-1) - u(t-3)} =", F);
inverseLaplace(F).result
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/systems.html

Topic

## Systems in the plane

`linearSystem` solves x′=Ax exactly: for a 2 by 2 matrix it names the kind of equilibrium, and for larger matrices it gives eAt and the stability. `planarSystem` takes a nonlinear system, finds every equilibrium in a box with proof, and classifies each from its linearisation.

```js
const s = linearSystem([[1, 2], [3, 2]]);
s.eigenvalues;      // ["-1", "4"]
s.kind;             // "saddle"
s.exponential;      // e^{At} as four formulas in t
s.solution([1, 0]); // ["2/5*exp(4*t) + 3/5*exp(-t)", "3/5*exp(4*t) - 3/5*exp(-t)"]

const pendulum = planarSystem(["y", "-sin(x) - y/2"], ["x", "y"]);
pendulum.equilibria({ x: [-4, 4], y: [-2, 2] });
// three records: saddle at (-π, 0), stable spiral at (0, 0), saddle at (π, 0)
```

### Linear systems

With τ=trA and Δ=detA, the eigenvalues are λ=21​(τ±τ2−4Δ​), and the origin is

| condition | kind |

| Δ | saddle: real eigenvalues of opposite signs |

| Δ>0, τ2>4Δ | node: stable if τ, unstable if τ>0 |

| Δ>0, τ20 |

| Δ>0, τ=0 | centre: closed orbits |

| Δ>0, τ2=4Δ | degenerate node, or a star when A is a multiple of the identity |

| Δ=0 | a line of equilibria |

The entries are rational, so the signs of τ, Δ and τ2−4Δ are decided exactly and the borderline cases are recognised for what they are.

The solution is x(t)=eAtx(0). For a 2 by 2 matrix, with μ=τ/2 and δ=μ2−Δ,

eAt=eμt(c(t)I+s(t)(A−μI)),(c,s)=⎩⎨⎧​(coshωt, sinh(ωt)/ω)(1, t)(cosωt, sin(ωt)/ω)​δ=ω2>0δ=0δ=−ω2<0,​
which follows from (A−μI)2=δI (Cayley-Hamilton).

### Larger systems

For an n by n matrix, eAt is the inverse Laplace transform of (sI−A)−1, because L{eAt}=(sI−A)−1. The Faddeev–LeVerrier recursion gives this inverse with exact rational coefficients: with M1​=I,

Mk​=AMk−1​+cn−k+1​I,cn−k​=−k1​tr(AMk​),(sI−A)−1=p(s)∑k=1n​Mk​sn−k​,
where p(s)=sn+cn−1​sn−1+⋯+c0​ is the characteristic polynomial. Each entry is then inverted by partial fractions. This works when p splits over the rationals into linear factors and quadratics. The result is checked: dtd​eAt=AeAt identically and eA⋅0=I, and `verified` reports it.

```js
const s3 = linearSystem([[0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1], [-6, -11, -6]]);
s3.characteristic;   // "s^3 + 6*s^2 + 11*s + 6 = 0"
s3.eigenvalues;      // ["-1", "-2", "-3"]
s3.stability;        // "asymptotically stable"
s3.solution([1, 0, 0])[0];   // "3*exp(-t) - 3*exp(-2*t) + exp(-3*t)"
linearSystem([[0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0]]).exponential[0];   // ["1", "t", "1/2*t^2"]
```

Stability is read from the real parts of the eigenvalues, whose signs are decided exactly. If every real part is negative, the system is asymptotically stable; if any is positive, it is unstable. Eigenvalues on the imaginary axis give stability that is not asymptotic, if each is semisimple, which is checked exactly by a rank. Otherwise the system is unstable: a repeated zero eigenvalue with a Jordan block makes eAt grow like a power of t. For other matrices, use the matrix exponential in the linear algebra package.

### Nonlinear systems

An equilibrium of x′=f(x,y), y′=g(x,y) is a common zero of f and g. `equilibria(box)` bisects the box, discards pieces where interval arithmetic shows f or g has no zero, and applies a Krawczyk test to the rest: when the test succeeds there is exactly one equilibrium in that piece. The returned list has `complete: true` when every part of the box was either proven empty or proven to hold exactly one equilibrium.

Near an equilibrium the system looks like its linearisation, x′=Jx with J the Jacobian matrix there. If no eigenvalue of J has zero real part (the equilibrium is hyperbolic), the nonlinear system has the same kind of equilibrium with the same stability (Hartman-Grobman). The trace and determinant of J are enclosed over the small box that holds the equilibrium, so a reported saddle, node or spiral is proven. When the linear part is a centre, the nonlinear terms decide, and the record says so.

Two tools settle such cases. `conserves(H)` checks that Hx​f+Hy​g is identically zero: a conserved quantity with a strict extremum at the equilibrium makes it a centre. `along(V)` gives V˙=Vx​f+Vy​g for a candidate Lyapunov function.

| call | returns |

| linearSystem([[a, b], [c, d]]) | { trace, determinant, discriminant, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, kind, stability, exponential, solution(x0) } |

| linearSystem(A), A n by n | { characteristic, eigenvalues, stability, exponential, verified, solution(x0) } |

| planarSystem([f, g], [x, y], { params }) | PlanarSystem |

| s.jacobian(), s.nullclines() | formulas |

| s.equilibria({ x: [a, b], y: [c, d] }) | records { point, unique, jacobian, trace, determinant, kind, stability, hyperbolic }, with complete on the list |

| s.conserves(H), s.along(V) | boolean, formula |

| s.orbit({ from, until }) | a Refinement like ode.solve |

### Try it

```js
// Linear systems across the trace-determinant plane.
for (const A of [[[1, 2], [3, 2]], [[-2, 1], [1, -2]], [[-1, -2], [2, -1]], [[0, 1], [-1, 0]], [[-1, 1], [0, -1]]]) {
  const s = linearSystem(A);
  PRINT(`${JSON.stringify(A)}: eigenvalues ${s.eigenvalues.join(" and ")} -> ${s.kind}`);
}
PRINT("rotation:", JSON.stringify(linearSystem([[0, 1], [-1, 0]]).exponential));
const big = linearSystem([[0, 1, 0], [-1, 0, 0], [0, 0, -2]]);
PRINT("3 by 3:", big.eigenvalues.join(", "), "->", big.stability, "; verified", big.verified);

// Competing species: every equilibrium in the box, proven and classified.
const species = planarSystem(["x*(3 - x - 2*y)", "y*(2 - x - y)"], ["x", "y"]);
const eq = species.equilibria({ x: [-1, 4], y: [-1, 4] });
PRINT("searched the whole box:", eq.complete);
for (const e of eq) PRINT(`  (${e.point.map((c) => c.low.toDecimal(4)).join(", ")}): ${e.kind}`);

// Predator and prey: the linear part at (1, 1) is a centre, and a conserved quantity shows the orbits close.
const lv = planarSystem(["x*(1 - y)", "y*(x - 1)"], ["x", "y"]);
lv.conserves("x - log(x) + y - log(y)");
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/seriessolutions.html

Topic

## Series solutions

Many equations of physics have no solution in elementary functions: Airy's, Bessel's, Legendre's. Their solutions are defined by power series. `seriesSolution` builds those series for y′′+p(x)y′+q(x)y=0 about a point, with exact rational coefficients, and says what kind of point it is.

```js
seriesSolution({ q: "-x", order: 7 });            // Airy: y'' = x y
// kind "ordinary", solutions "1 + 1/6*x^3 + 1/180*x^6 + …" and "x + 1/12*x^4 + 1/504*x^7 + …"

seriesSolution({ p: "1/x", q: "(x^2 - 1/4)/x^2" });   // Bessel of order 1/2
// kind "regular singular", indicial "r^2 - 1/4 = 0", exponents [1/2, -1/2], two series
```

### Ordinary points

If p and q are analytic at x0​, every solution is a power series ∑an​(x−x0​)n there, and it converges at least as far as the nearest singularity of p or q in the complex plane. Substituting the series and matching powers gives a recurrence that determines every an​ from a0​ and a1​:

(n+2)(n+1)an+2​=−k=0∑n​(pk​(n−k+1)an−k+1​+qk​an−k​).
The two solutions returned are the ones with (y,y′)(x0​)=(1,0) and (0,1). `radius` estimates the distance to the nearest singularity.

### Regular singular points and Frobenius

If p has at most a simple pole and q at most a double pole at x0​, the point is a regular singular point. Write xp(x)=∑Pk​xk and x2q(x)=∑Qk​xk (taking x0​=0). Frobenius' method looks for y=xr∑an​xn; the lowest power gives the indicial equation

r(r−1)+P0​r+Q0​=0,
and for each root r the recurrence

[(n+r)(n+r−1)+P0​(n+r)+Q0​]an​=−k=1∑n​(Pk​(n−k+r)+Qk​)an−k​.
The larger root always gives a series. The smaller root gives a second one unless the roots are equal or differ by a whole number, in which case the bracket on the left can vanish for some n; then the second solution contains logx, and `notes` says so. (When the right side happens to vanish too, the series exists after all, as for Bessel's equation of order one half.)

A point where the poles are worse is an irregular singular point, and the method does not apply.

### A proven remainder

A truncated series is only useful with a bound on what was cut off. Each solution y=(x−x0​)rg(x), g=∑an​(x−x0​)n, carries one: `remainder(ρ)` returns a rational B with

​g(x)−n≤N∑​an​(x−x0​)n​≤Bfor all complex x with ∣x−x0​∣≤ρ,
for any ρ below `provenRadius`. `enclose(x)` evaluates the partial sum at a rational point and puts that bound on either side.

```js
const cos = seriesSolution({ q: "1", order: 12 }).solutions[0];   // y'' + y = 0, y(0) = 1, y'(0) = 0
cos.remainder(1).bound;        // 447/1000000000000: the terms beyond x^12 are below 4.47e-10 on the unit disc
const e = cos.enclose("1/2");  // { partial, bound, low, high }
e.low.toDecimal(15), e.high.toDecimal(15);   // both 0.877582561890372…: cos(1/2) to 13 places, proven
```

The proof is the classical convergence argument made quantitative. Take x0​=0. First, a radius: the reciprocals of the roots of the denominators of p and q are bounded by root squaring (Graeffe) and Fujiwara's bound, in exact arithmetic, giving R with no singular point in 0; that is `provenRadius`, within about one percent of the true distance. Second, for a radius s, numbers MP​,MQ​ with ∣Pk​∣≤MP​/sk and ∣Qk​∣≤MQ​/sk for all k≥1: the first hundred or so coefficients are used exactly and the rest are bounded by a majorant of the form (1−x/R)−m. Third, the recurrence. With bn​=∣an​∣sn and cj​=MP​(∣r∣+j)+MQ​ it gives

n(n+δ)bn​≤Sn​:=j<n∑​cj​bj​,Sn+1​≤Sn​(1+εn​),εn​=n(n+δ)cn​​,
where δ=2r−1+P0​, because the bracket in the recurrence equals n(n+δ). SN+1​ is known exactly from the coefficients already computed, and εn​ decreases to 0. So for ∣x∣≤ρ the tail ∑n>N​bn​(ρ/s)n is at most a few explicit terms plus a geometric series, once (1+εn​)ρ/s<1. Several values of s are tried and the smallest bound kept. Every step is rational arithmetic rounded upward.

The bound covers the series g; the factor (x−x0​)r is explicit. Near the edge of the disc a bound still exists but is weak, as it must be: the series itself converges slowly there.

### Checking a series

The coefficients are exact, and a partial sum is a polynomial whose value at a rational point is an exact rational. Comparing it with the validated solution of the same initial value problem shows the true truncation error next to the proven bound, as in the box below.

| call | returns |

| seriesSolution({ p, q, about = 0, order = 8, x = "x" }) | { about, kind, indicial, exponents, solutions, notes, radius, provenRadius } |

| solutions[i] | { exponent, coefficients, text, remainder, enclose }, coefficients exact |

| solutions[i].remainder(ρ) | { radius, terms, bound, approx, text }: a proven bound for the terms left out, on the disc of radius ρ |

| solutions[i].enclose(x) | { partial, bound, low, high, exponent }: the series factor at a rational x |

### Try it

```js
// Airy's equation y'' = x·y about 0.
const airy = seriesSolution({ q: "-x", order: 12 });
PRINT(airy.kind, "point");
for (const s of airy.solutions) PRINT("  ", s.text);

// The partial sum at x = 1 against the validated solution of y'' = x·y, y(0) = 1, y'(0) = 0.
const a = airy.solutions[0].coefficients;
let partial = new Rational(0);
for (const c of a) partial = partial.add(c);            // x = 1: just add the coefficients
const exact = ode.solve({ f: ["v", "x*y"], vars: ["y", "v"], time: "x", y0: [1, 0], until: 1 }).exact().final[0];
PRINT("partial sum at 1:", partial.toDecimal(12), " validated:", exact.low.toDecimal(12));
PRINT("truncation error about", exact.low.subtract(partial).toDecimal(10));
PRINT("proven bound on the unit disc:", airy.solutions[0].remainder(1).text);
const at1 = airy.solutions[0].enclose(1);
PRINT("so y(1) lies in [", at1.low.toDecimal(12), ",", at1.high.toDecimal(12), "]");

// Bessel's equation of order 0: equal exponents, so one series and a logarithm.
const j0 = seriesSolution({ p: "1/x", q: "1", order: 8 });
PRINT(j0.kind, " indicial:", j0.indicial);
PRINT("  J0 =", j0.solutions[0].text);
PRINT("  note:", j0.notes[0]);

// Legendre's equation with n = 2: one solution is a polynomial, and the radius is 1.
const leg = seriesSolution({ p: "-2*x/(1 - x^2)", q: "6/(1 - x^2)", order: 8 });
PRINT("Legendre:", leg.solutions[0].text, "  radius", leg.radius.toFixed(3), "  proven radius", leg.provenRadius.toNumber().toFixed(3));
PRINT("  second solution,", leg.solutions[1].remainder("1/2").text);
PRINT("  and", leg.solutions[1].remainder("9/10").text);
seriesSolution({ p: "1/x^2", q: "1" }).kind;
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/characteristics.html

Topic

## First-order equations: characteristics

`transport` solves ut​+cux​+ku=s with u(x,0)=f(x) along characteristics: a closed formula where there is one, a certified value at a point otherwise, and a plain statement of where characteristics cross and the solution stops being a function.

```js
const u = transport({ speed: 2, initial: "exp(-x^2)" });
u.formula;            // "exp(-(x - 2*t)^2)"
u.characteristics;    // "x - 2*t = const"
u.at(1, "1/2").value; // exactly 1: the foot of the characteristic is x = 0
u.residual(3, 1);     // [0, 0]: the formula put back into the equation

const b = transport({ speed: "u", initial: "exp(-x^2)", interval: [-4, 4] });
b.crossing.time;      // [1.165821…]: the breaking time sqrt(e/2)
b.at(1, 2);           // refuses: characteristics have crossed
```

### The idea

Follow a curve x(t) with dx/dt=c. Along it, by the chain rule, dtd​u(x(t),t)=ut​+cux​, so the partial differential equation becomes the ordinary one du/dt=s−ku. With constant k and s,

u(x,t)=f(ξ)e−kt+ks​(1−e−kt)(f(ξ)+st when k=0),
where ξ is the foot: the point of the line t=0 from which the characteristic through (x,t) started. Solving the equation is finding the foot.

- Constant speed. The characteristics are the parallel lines x−ct=ξ, and u=f(x−ct): the initial profile moves at speed c unchanged.

- Speed ax+b. dx/dt=ax+b gives ξ=(x+b/a)e−at−b/a, again a closed formula.

- Any other c(x,t). The foot is the value at time 0 of the solution of dx/dt=c(x,t) through (x,t), followed backwards by the validated ODE solver. The result is an enclosure of the foot, and so of u.

In all three cases the characteristics are solutions of one ordinary differential equation, and two solutions through the same point are the same solution: they never cross, and u is defined for all time. Where there is a closed formula, `residual(x, t)` differentiates it and encloses ut​+cux​+ku−s at a point, which is a check that does not go through characteristics at all.

### When the speed depends on u

For ut​+c(u)ux​=0, such as Burgers' equation ut​+uux​=0, u is still constant along each characteristic, so each one is a straight line whose slope is set by the value it carries:

x=ξ+F(ξ)t,F(ξ)=c(f(ξ)).
Now the lines can meet. Two neighbours starting at ξ and ξ+dξ cross when 1+F′(ξ)t=0, so the first crossing is at the breaking time

tb​=minξ​F′(ξ)−1​
if F′ is negative somewhere, and never if F′≥0 (faster values ahead of slower ones: a rarefaction). Past tb​ the method would assign several values to one point; the equation then has no classical solution, and `at` refuses instead of returning one of them.

With `interval: [a, b]` the least value of F′ over starting points in [a,b] is enclosed by subdivision, which gives an enclosure of tb​ for those characteristics. Before the breaking time, ξ↦ξ+F(ξ)t is increasing, so the foot is its one root, found by bisection. Without an interval the claim is local: `at` first proves 1+F′(ξ)t>0 on the bracket it found, and refuses where it cannot.

| call | returns |

| transport({ speed, decay = 0, source = 0, initial, interval, order = 8, tol = "1e-8" }) | { kind, characteristics, foot, formula, crossing, at, residual }; also pde.transport |

| u.at(x, t) | { value, foot }: RationalIntervals (single numbers when the arithmetic is exact) |

| u.residual(x, t) | an enclosure of the equation's left side minus right side from the closed formula |

| u.crossing | { never: true \| false \| null, time, reason } |

### Try it

```js
// A pulse carried at speed 2.
const u = transport({ speed: 2, initial: "exp(-x^2)" });
PRINT("u =", u.formula, "  on", u.characteristics);
PRINT("u(1, 1/2) =", u.at(1, "1/2").value.low.toString(), "  residual at (3, 1):", u.residual(3, 1).low.toString());

// Decay and a source; a speed that grows with x.
const w = transport({ speed: -1, decay: 3, source: 2, initial: "sin(x)" });
PRINT("u =", w.formula);
const s = transport({ speed: "x", initial: "1/(1 + x^2)" });
PRINT("speed x: foot", s.foot, " u =", s.formula);

// A speed with no closed foot formula here: followed back by the validated ODE solver.
const v = transport({ speed: "t*x", initial: "x^2" });
const p = v.at(1, 1);
PRINT("speed t·x: foot of (1, 1) in [" + p.foot.low.toDecimal(10) + ", " + p.foot.high.toDecimal(10) + "],  exp(-1/2) =", Math.exp(-0.5));

// Burgers' equation: the wave steepens and breaks at sqrt(e/2).
const b = transport({ speed: "u", initial: "exp(-x^2)", interval: [-4, 4] });
PRINT("breaking time in [" + b.crossing.time.low.toDecimal(7) + ", " + b.crossing.time.high.toDecimal(7) + "],  sqrt(e/2) =", Math.sqrt(Math.E / 2));
PRINT("u(1, 1/2) =", b.at(1, "1/2").value.low.toDecimal(12));
try { b.at(1, 2); } catch (e) { PRINT("u(1, 2):", e.message); }
u.formula;
```
