Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/curves.html

Topic

## Curves: length, curvature, torsion

A curve is a list of two or three formulas in one parameter. `curve` differentiates them and returns what a first course in differential geometry computes, each as a formula and as a certified value at a point: speed and arc length, the Frenet frame, curvature and torsion, the osculating circle and the evolute.

```js
const helix = curve(["cos(t)", "sin(t)", "t/2"], "t");
helix.speed();              // "sqrt(5/4)"
helix.curvature();          // "4/5"
helix.torsion();            // "2/5"
helix.length([0, "2*pi"]);  // an interval around π√5

const a = helix.at(1);      // every number an interval
a.tangent; a.normal; a.binormal;
a.curvature;                // [4/5, 4/5]
a.radius; a.centre;         // the osculating circle
```

It is also available as `import { curve, surface, metric } from "@ratmath/analytic/geometry"`.

### Speed and arc length

For r(t) the velocity is r′(t) and the speed is ∣r′(t)∣. The length of the curve between t=a and t=b is

L=∫ab​∣r′(t)∣dt.
`length` encloses that integral; the ends may be formulas such as `"2*pi"`. A curve is regular where the speed is not zero. At a point where the velocity may vanish, such as the cusp of (t2,t3) at 0, there is no tangent and `at` refuses.

### Curvature

Curvature measures how fast the unit tangent T=r′/∣r′∣ turns per unit of length: κ=∣dT/ds∣. In terms of the parameter,

κ=∣r′∣3∣r′×r′′∣​in space,κ=(x′2+y′2)3/2x′y′′−y′x′′​in the plane.
In the plane the curvature has a sign: positive where the curve turns to the left. A circle of radius R has curvature 1/R, a line has curvature 0.

The osculating circle at a point is the circle that fits the curve best there: it passes through the point with the same tangent and the same curvature. Its radius is 1/∣κ∣ and its centre is r+N/κ, where N is the unit normal. The centres trace the evolute; `evolute()` returns it as another curve, so the evolute of a parabola is one line of code.

The integral of the curvature against arc length is the total turning of the tangent. For a simple closed curve in the plane it is 2π, whatever the shape; `totalCurvature` encloses it.

### The Frenet frame and torsion

In space the unit tangent T, the principal normal N=T′/∣T′∣ and the binormal B=T×N form a frame that travels with the curve. The Frenet formulas say how it turns:

T′=κN,N′=−κT+τB,B′=−τN(derivatives in arc length).
The torsion τ measures how fast the curve leaves its osculating plane:

τ=∣r′×r′′∣2(r′×r′′)⋅r′′′​.
A curve lies in a plane exactly when its torsion is zero, and a curve with constant curvature and constant torsion is a helix. Where the curvature may be zero the normal and binormal are not defined, and `at` reports them as `null`.

### Formulas that come out readable

The formulas are tidied by `tidy`, which writes a formula as a quotient of polynomials in its variables and function calls, uses sin2+cos2=1 and P​2=P, and cancels the common factor. It is exported for use on your own formulas: `format(tidy(parse("(x^2 - 1)/(x - 1)")))` is `"x + 1"`.

| call | returns |

| curve(components, parameter = "t", { params }) | Curve, in the plane or in space |

| c.position, c.velocity, c.acceleration | formulas |

| c.speed(), c.curvature(), c.torsion() | formulas |

| c.evolute() | Curve (plane curves) |

| c.length([a, b], { digits = 12 }), c.totalCurvature([a, b]) | RationalInterval |

| c.at(t, { digits = 15 }) | { point, velocity, speed, tangent, normal, binormal, curvature, torsion, radius, centre } |

| tidy(tree) | the tidied formula tree |

### Try it

```js
// An ellipse: curvature at the ends of the axes, the osculating circles there,
// its length (an elliptic integral, enclosed) and its total curvature.
const ellipse = curve(["2*cos(t)", "sin(t)"], "t");
PRINT("curvature:", ellipse.curvature());
for (const t of [0, "pi/2"]) {
  const a = ellipse.at(t);
  PRINT(`t = ${t}: curvature ${a.curvature.low.toDecimal(6)}, circle of radius ${a.radius.low.toDecimal(6)} centred at (${a.centre.map((c) => c.low.toDecimal(4)).join(", ")})`);
}
PRINT("length:", ellipse.length([0, "2*pi"]).low.toDecimal(10));
PRINT("total curvature:", ellipse.totalCurvature([0, "2*pi"]).low.toDecimal(8), "= 2π");
PRINT("evolute:", ellipse.evolute().position.join(" , "));

// A space curve whose torsion changes sign.
const twisted = curve(["t", "t^2", "t^3"], "t");
PRINT("torsion:", twisted.torsion());
PRINT("binormal at t = 1:", twisted.at(1).binormal.map((c) => c.low.toDecimal(5)).join(", "));
`the helix (cos t, sin t, t/2) has curvature ${curve(["cos(t)", "sin(t)", "t/2"]).curvature()} and torsion ${curve(["cos(t)", "sin(t)", "t/2"]).torsion()}`;
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/surfaces.html

Topic

## Surfaces and curvature

A surface is three formulas in two parameters. `surface` returns its two fundamental forms, its normal, and its Gaussian, mean and principal curvatures, as formulas and as certified values, and says what kind of point each point is.

```js
const torus = surface(["(2 + cos(v))*cos(u)", "(2 + cos(v))*sin(u)", "sin(v)"], ["u", "v"]);
torus.first();        // { E: "cos(v)^2 + 4*cos(v) + 4", F: "0", G: "1" }
torus.gaussian();     // "cos(v)/(cos(v) + 2)"
torus.at(0, 0).kind;      // "elliptic"    the outer rim
torus.at(0, "pi").kind;   // "hyperbolic"  the inner rim
torus.area({ u: [0, "2*pi"], v: [0, "2*pi"] });   // an interval around 8π²
```

### The first fundamental form

With r(u,v) the surface and ru​,rv​ its partial derivatives,

E=ru​⋅ru​,F=ru​⋅rv​,G=rv​⋅rv​.
These three functions hold everything that can be measured inside the surface. A curve (u(t),v(t)) on it has speed Eu′2+2Fu′v′+Gv′2​; the angle between two directions comes from the same form; and area is

A=∬EG−F2​dudv.
The parametrisation is regular where EG−F2>0. At a point where that fails (the poles of a sphere in latitude and longitude) `at` refuses.

### The second fundamental form and curvature

With unit normal n=(ru​×rv​)/∣ru​×rv​∣,

L=ruu​⋅n,M=ruv​⋅n,N=rvv​⋅n.
Cut the surface with a plane through the normal: the curvature of the section is the normal curvature in that direction. Its largest and smallest values over all directions are the principal curvatures k1​≤k2​, and

K=k1​k2​=EG−F2LN−M2​,H=2k1​+k2​​=2(EG−F2)EN−2FM+GL​,k1,2​=H∓H2−K​.
K is the Gaussian curvature and H the mean curvature. The sign of H depends on which way the normal points; K does not.

| kind | condition | the surface near the point |

| elliptic | K>0 | lies on one side of its tangent plane, like a dome |

| hyperbolic | K | crosses its tangent plane, like a saddle |

| parabolic | K=0, not planar | curved in one direction only, like a cylinder |

| planar | L=M=N=0 | flat to second order |

An enclosure can prove K>0 or K. It cannot prove K=0, so parabolic and planar are reported only when the formulas vanish exactly at the point; otherwise `kind` is `null`.

### The Theorema Egregium

K is defined through the normal, which is about how the surface sits in space. Gauss found that it can be computed from E,F,G alone: bend a sheet of paper without stretching it and K stays 0 everywhere. `intrinsicGaussian()` computes K from the first form by way of the Christoffel symbols and the curvature tensor, and it agrees with `gaussian()`.

Because of that, the curvature makes sense for a `metric` with no surface behind it; see [Geodesics and Gauss-Bonnet](https://ratmath.com/analytic/geodesics.html).

| call | returns |

| surface(components, [u, v], { params }) | Surface (a Metric with a normal) |

| s.first(), s.second(), s.normal() | { E, F, G }, { L, M, N }, r_u × r_v, as formulas |

| s.gaussian(), s.mean(), s.intrinsicGaussian() | formulas |

| s.at(u, v, { digits = 15 }) | { point, normal, E, F, G, L, M, N, gaussian, mean, principal, kind } |

| s.area(region, { digits = 8 }), s.totalCurvature(region) | RationalInterval; region { u: [a, b], v: [lo(u), hi(u)] } |

### Try it

```js
// A monkey saddle and a paraboloid, classified point by point.
const saddle = surface(["u", "v", "u^3 - 3*u*v^2"], ["u", "v"]);
PRINT("K =", saddle.gaussian());
for (const [u, v] of [[1, 0], [0, 1], [0, 0]]) {
  const a = saddle.at(u, v);
  PRINT(`(${u}, ${v}): K in [${a.gaussian.low.toDecimal(5)}, ${a.gaussian.high.toDecimal(5)}], ${a.kind}`);
}

const bowl = surface(["u", "v", "u^2 + v^2"], ["u", "v"]);
const b = bowl.at(1, 0);
PRINT("bowl at (1, 0): principal curvatures", b.principal.map((k) => k.low.toDecimal(6)).join(" and "), "->", b.kind);
PRINT("the same K from the metric alone:", bowl.intrinsicGaussian() === bowl.gaussian());

// Area of the torus, 8π² = 78.9568...
const torus = surface(["(2 + cos(v))*cos(u)", "(2 + cos(v))*sin(u)", "sin(v)"], ["u", "v"]);
PRINT("torus area:", torus.area({ u: [0, "2*pi"], v: [0, "2*pi"] }).low.toDecimal(6));
PRINT("total curvature of the torus:", torus.totalCurvature({ u: [0, "2*pi"], v: [0, "2*pi"] }).high.toDecimal(6), "(it is 0)");
`torus: K = ${torus.gaussian()}`;
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/geodesics.html

Topic

## Geodesics and Gauss-Bonnet

The geometry inside a surface needs only its first fundamental form. A `metric` is that form on its own; a `surface` is a metric too. Both give Christoffel symbols, geodesics as validated solutions of their differential equations, parallel transport, geodesic curvature, and the Gauss-Bonnet theorem as a checked statement.

```js
const sphere = surface(["cos(u)*sin(v)", "sin(u)*sin(v)", "cos(v)"], ["u", "v"]);
sphere.christoffel();     // { u_uv: "cos(v)/sin(v)", v_uu: "-(sin(v)*cos(v))", ... }

const plane = metric({ E: "1/v^2", F: 0, G: "1/v^2" }, ["u", "v"]);   // the hyperbolic half-plane
plane.gaussian();         // "-1"

const g = plane.geodesic({ from: [0, 1], direction: [1, 0], until: 1 });
g.quick.value;            // a preview at once: { t, y: [u, v, u', v'] }
g.exact().final;          // certified enclosures of u, v, u', v' at the end

sphere.gaussBonnet({ u: [0, 1], v: [1, 2] }).agree;   // true
```

### Christoffel symbols

Write the metric as g11​=E, g12​=g21​=F, g22​=G and its inverse as gkl. The Christoffel symbols

Γijk​=21​l∑​gkl(∂i​glj​+∂j​gli​−∂l​gij​)
say how the coordinate directions turn from point to point. `christoffel()` lists the six different ones under keys such as `u_uv` for Γuvu​.

### Geodesics

A geodesic is a curve that does not turn within the surface: its acceleration has no tangential part. In coordinates,

u′′=−i,j∑​Γiju​xi′xj′,v′′=−i,j∑​Γijv​xi′xj′,(x1,x2)=(u,v).
Geodesics are the straight lines of the surface: great circles on a sphere, and in the half-plane model vertical lines and half-circles centred on the boundary. A short enough piece of a geodesic is the shortest path between its ends.

`geodesic` solves this system from a point in a direction. Like every [differential equation here](https://ratmath.com/analytic/odes.html) it answers twice: `quick` is a floating-point preview, and `exact()` is a validated solution whose every value is an enclosure. Certified steps of this system take about a second each, so the defaults are modest (six digits); pass `order` and `tol` for more. With `{ unit: true }` the direction is scaled to unit speed, and the parameter is arc length.

### Parallel transport

Carrying a tangent vector V along a curve c(t) without turning it within the surface means solving

Vk′=−i,j∑​Γijk​ci′Vj.
Transport keeps lengths and angles. Carried around a closed curve a vector comes back rotated, and on a surface the rotation equals the integral of K over the region enclosed. Around the circle of colatitude φ on the unit sphere that is 2π(1−cosφ), which is why a Foucault pendulum away from the poles does not return to its plane in a day. `transport` reports the transported vector and the angle.

### Geodesic curvature

The curvature of a curve on a surface splits into a part along the normal and a part within the surface. The second is the geodesic curvature kg​: how much someone walking on the surface has to steer. For c(t)=(u(t),v(t)),

kg​=∣c′∣3EG−F2​(u′Av−v′Au)​,Ak=xk′′+i,j∑​Γijk​xi′xj′.
It is zero exactly along geodesics. The sign is positive when the curve turns towards the side to which u rotates into v.

### The Gauss-Bonnet theorem

For a region R on a surface bounded by a simple closed curve made of smooth pieces,

∬R​KdA+∮∂R​kg​ds+i∑​θi​=2π,
where the θi​ are the exterior angles at the corners. For a triangle with geodesic sides the middle term vanishes and the theorem says that the angles add to π+∬KdA: more than π on a sphere, less on a saddle.

`gaussBonnet(region)` checks the theorem on the image of the region {a≤u≤b, lo(u)≤v≤hi(u)}. The three terms are enclosed separately: a double integral, one integral per side, and an angle per corner measured with the metric. It reports each, their sum, and whether the sum contains 2π. The theorem holds, so `agree` is a check of the computation and a way to see how the three terms trade off as the region changes. The patch must be regular up to its boundary.

| call | returns |

| metric({ E, F, G }, [u, v], { params }) | Metric |

| m.christoffel(), m.gaussian() | formulas |

| m.geodesic({ from, direction, until, unit, order, tol }) | a Refinement: quick, exact() an ODESolution in (u, v, u′, v′) |

| m.transport(path, [a, b], vector, { order, tol }) | { start, vector, length, lengthAfter, angle, solution }; path { u: "…", v: "…" } in t |

| m.geodesicCurvature(path, t) | a formula, or with t a RationalInterval |

| m.gaussBonnet(region, { digits = 7 }) | { statement, curvature, boundary, angles, total, expected, agree } |

| m.area(region), m.totalCurvature(region) | RationalInterval |

### Try it

```js
// Gauss-Bonnet on a patch of the unit sphere (u is longitude, v colatitude).
const sphere = surface(["cos(u)*sin(v)", "sin(u)*sin(v)", "cos(v)"], ["u", "v"]);
const gb = sphere.gaussBonnet({ u: [0, 1], v: [1, 2] });
PRINT(gb.statement);
PRINT("  curvature inside:", gb.curvature.value.low.toDecimal(7));
for (const p of gb.boundary.pieces) PRINT(`  side ${p.side}:`, p.value.low.toDecimal(7));
PRINT("  exterior angles: ", gb.angles.value.low.toDecimal(7));
PRINT("  total:", gb.total.low.toDecimal(6), "to", gb.total.high.toDecimal(6), " 2π inside:", gb.agree);

// The same in the hyperbolic half-plane, where K = -1.
const plane = metric({ E: "1/v^2", F: 0, G: "1/v^2" }, ["u", "v"]);
const hb = plane.gaussBonnet({ u: [0, 1], v: [1, "2 + u"] });
PRINT("hyperbolic patch: curvature", hb.curvature.value.low.toDecimal(6), "sides", hb.boundary.value.low.toDecimal(6), "angles", hb.angles.value.low.toDecimal(6), "agree:", hb.agree);

// A geodesic of the half-plane from (0, 1) heading right is the unit circle: u^2 + v^2 = 1.
const g = plane.geodesic({ from: [0, 1], direction: [1, 0], until: 2 });
const q = g.quick.value;
const end = [q.y[0].at(-1), q.y[1].at(-1)];
PRINT("preview at s = 2:", end.map((x) => x.toFixed(6)).join(", "), " u^2 + v^2 =", (end[0] ** 2 + end[1] ** 2).toFixed(8));
const sol = plane.geodesic({ from: [0, 1], direction: [1, 0], until: "1/8" }).exact();
PRINT("certified at s = 1/8: u in", sol.final[0].low.toDecimal(8), "to", sol.final[0].high.toDecimal(8), " (tanh(1/8) = 0.12435300...)");
`Christoffel symbols of the half-plane: ${JSON.stringify(plane.christoffel())}`;
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/floats.html

Numerical methods

## Floating point, exactly

This library returns proven answers and so avoids floating-point arithmetic for its results. That makes it a good place to study floating point: every double is an exact rational number, Core can hold it, and so the rounding error of each operation is a number that can be computed exactly, not estimated.

```js
exactOf(0.1);              // 3602879701896397/36028797018963968   what the double 0.1 IS
floatParts(0.1, "0.1");    // sign, exponent, mantissa, bits, ulp, and the error against the 0.1 that was typed
floatOp("+", 0.1, 0.2);    // { result: 0.30000000000000004, exact, error, relativeError, exactlyRepresentable: false }

roundoff("(1 - cos(x))/x^2", { x: 1e-8 });
// { float: 0, exact: [0.5, 0.5], relativeError: 1, digitsLost: 16, steps: […] }
```

These and the other numerical methods are also at `@ratmath/analytic/methods`.

### What a double is

A double is ±m⋅2e with a 53-bit mantissa 1≤m and an exponent −1022≤e≤1023 (plus zero, subnormals, infinities and NaN). So it is a fraction whose denominator is a power of two. The decimal 0.1 is not such a fraction, and the double written `0.1` is the nearest one that is:

0.1double​=2553602879701896397​=0.1+1801439850948198401​.
`floatParts` shows the three bit fields, the exact value, and the ulp: the gap to the next double. Rounding to nearest makes a relative error of at most 2−53≈1.1×10−16, the unit roundoff.

### One operation

IEEE arithmetic computes the exact result of a∘b on the two doubles and rounds it to the nearest double. `floatOp` gives both: `exact` is the true sum, difference, product or quotient of the two doubles as a rational, `result` is what the machine returns, and `error` is their exact difference. So 0.1+0.2=0.3 stops being a mystery: the two inputs are each slightly above their decimals, their exact sum is not a double, and it rounds up.

### Cancellation

Each operation is accurate to one part in 1016. A calculation is not. Subtracting two nearly equal numbers gives a small result whose leading digits have cancelled, and the rounding errors already present in the inputs are then large in proportion. `roundoff` follows a whole formula both ways, in doubles and with certified enclosures of the true value at the same inputs, and lists every subexpression with its relative error. The step where the error jumps is the step to rewrite:

x21−cosx​=x22sin2(x/2)​.
The two sides are equal; at x=10−8 the left gives 0 in doubles and the right gives 0.5, correct to the last bit.

| call | returns |

| exactOf(x) | the Rational equal to the double x |

| nearestDouble(q) | the double nearest a Rational, ties to even |

| floatParts(x, intended) | { sign, exponent, mantissa, bits, exact, ulp, next, previous, subnormal, intended, error, relativeError } |

| floatOp(op, a, b) | { result, exact, error, relativeError, exactlyRepresentable } |

| roundoff(formula, inputs) | { float, exact, error, relativeError, digitsLost, steps } |

### Try it

```js
// What is stored when you type 0.1?
const p = floatParts(0.1, "0.1");
PRINT("bits:    ", p.bits);
PRINT("exact:   ", p.exact.toString());
PRINT("too big by", p.error.toString(), "=", p.error.toNumber().toExponential(3));

// 0.1 + 0.2: the exact sum of the two doubles, and what the machine returns.
const s = floatOp("+", 0.1, 0.2);
PRINT("0.1 + 0.2 =", s.result, " exact sum of the doubles:", s.exact.toDecimal(22));
PRINT("rounding moved it by", s.error.toNumber().toExponential(3), "(half an ulp is", (floatParts(0.3).ulp.toNumber() / 2).toExponential(3) + ")");

// Cancellation, step by step.
for (const formula of ["(1 - cos(x))/x^2", "2*sin(x/2)^2/x^2"]) {
  const r = roundoff(formula, { x: 1e-8 });
  PRINT(`${formula} at x = 1e-8: double ${r.float}, true ${r.exact.low.toDecimal(12)}, digits lost ${r.digitsLost}`);
  for (const step of r.steps) PRINT(`    ${step.expression.padEnd(22)} ${String(step.float).padEnd(24)} relative error ${step.relativeError === null ? "-" : step.relativeError.toExponential(1)}`);
}

// The quadratic formula for x^2 - 1e8 x + 1: the small root, two ways.
const naive = roundoff("(b - sqrt(b^2 - 4))/2", { b: 1e8 });
const stable = roundoff("2/(b + sqrt(b^2 - 4))", { b: 1e8 });
`small root: naive ${naive.float} (lost ${naive.digitsLost} digits), rewritten ${stable.float} (lost ${stable.digitsLost})`;
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/rootmethods.html

Numerical methods

## Root-finding methods

Bisection, fixed-point iteration, Newton's method and the secant method, each run in doubles the way a textbook runs it, with its table of iterations. Because the root is also known with certainty (from [zeros](https://ratmath.com/analytic/zeros.html)), every row carries the true error, and the order of convergence is measured, not assumed.

```js
const n = newton("x^2 - 2", 1);
n.iterations;   // [{ n, x, fx, dfx, error }, …]   error = |x − √2|, the real one
n.order;        // 1.9998   observed
n.root;         // the certified root the errors are measured against

bisection("x^2 - 2", [1, 2], { steps: 10 }).iterations;   // each with bound (b − a)/2ⁿ⁺¹ and the true error
secant("x^3 - x - 1", 1, 2).order;                         // about 1.6
fixedPoint("cos(x)", 1).multiplier;                        // g′ at the fixed point: −0.6736…
```

### Order of convergence

With en​=∣xn​−x∗∣, a method has order p when en+1​≈Cenp​. Order 1 (with C) gains a fixed number of digits each step; order 2 doubles the number of correct digits each step. From three successive errors,

p≈log(en​/en−1​)log(en+1​/en​)​,
which is what `order` reports, using the last errors that are still well above rounding.

| method | step | order | needs |

| bisection | halve the bracket, keep the half with the sign change | 1, with C=21​ | a sign change; always converges |

| fixed point | x←g(x) | 1, with C=∣g′(x∗)∣ | ∣g′(x∗)∣Expand f about xn​ and evaluate at the root: 0=f(xn​)+f′(xn​)(x∗−xn​)+21​f′′(ξ)(x∗−xn​)2. Dividing by f′(xn​) and rearranging,

xn+1​−x∗=2f′(xn​)f′′(ξ)​(xn​−x∗)2.
At a multiple root f′(x∗)=0, the argument fails, and the observed order drops to 1: try `newton("(x - 1)^2", 2)`.

### Newton's method with fractions

With `{ exact: true }`, `newton` works the way it would by hand with fractions: every iterate is an exact Core Rational, so there is no rounding floor at all. For x2−2 from 1 the iterates are 23​,1217​,408577​,470832665857​, the convergents of 2​ that the Babylonians used. The price shows in `denominatorDigits`: the denominators double in length each step, just as the correct digits do. `floats` holds the double-precision iterates from the same start, so the two can be compared row by row. This needs f built from +, −, ×, ÷ and integer powers, so that f(x) and f′(x) are fractions; the default is 6 steps.

### Fixed points and the multiplier

For x←g(x), xn+1​−x∗=g(xn​)−g(x∗)≈g′(x∗)(xn​−x∗). So each step multiplies the error by about g′(x∗). `fixedPoint` returns an enclosure of that multiplier at the certified fixed point and the observed `ratio` of successive errors, which should agree with it. The proof of convergence by the contraction principle is in [recursive sequences](https://ratmath.com/analytic/sequences.html).

### What the true error shows

The root the errors are measured against is the one the method actually converges to. A sign-changing bracket can hold several roots: bisection on (x−1)(x−6)(x−9) over [0,10] keeps [0,5] after the first step and closes in on 1, not on the root 6 nearest the first midpoint, so `bisection` takes the certified root inside its last bracket. When that root is known only to a small interval, `error` is an upper bound for the distance, not the exact distance.

A program cannot know its error, so in practice the step size ∣xn+1​−xn​∣ or the residual ∣f(xn​)∣ stands in for it. Here the error itself is in the table, measured against a root enclosed to 25 digits, so the stand-ins can be judged. The last rows show the floor that rounding sets: the error stops near 10−16 times the size of the root however many more steps are taken.

| call | returns |

| bisection(f, [a, b], { steps = 20 }) | { iterations: [{ n, a, b, x, fx, bound, error }], root, order } |

| newton(f, x0, { steps = 10 }) | { iterations: [{ n, x, fx, dfx, error }], root, order, derivative } |

| newton(f, x0, { exact: true, steps = 6 }) | the same with x, fx and dfx as Rationals, plus denominatorDigits on each row and floats, the double iterates |

| secant(f, x0, x1, { steps = 12 }) | { iterations: [{ n, x, fx, error }], root, order } |

| fixedPoint(g, x0, { steps = 25 }) | { iterations, root, multiplier, ratio, order } |

### Try it

```js
// Three methods on x^3 - x - 1 = 0, errors measured against the certified root.
const f = "x^3 - x - 1";
const table = (r) => r.iterations.map((row) => (row.error === null ? "?" : row.error.toExponential(1))).join("  ");

const b = bisection(f, [1, 2], { steps: 8 });
PRINT("bisection errors:", table(b));
PRINT("   bounds:       ", b.iterations.map((row) => row.bound.toExponential(1)).join("  "));

const n = newton(f, 1.5);
PRINT("Newton errors:   ", table(n), "  observed order", n.order.toFixed(3));

const s = secant(f, 1, 2);
PRINT("secant errors:   ", table(s), "  observed order", s.order.toFixed(3));
PRINT("root:", n.root.low.toDecimal(20));

// Fixed-point iteration: the error shrinks by the multiplier each step.
const c = fixedPoint("cos(x)", 1, { steps: 30 });
PRINT(`x = cos(x): multiplier g'(x*) = ${c.multiplier.low.toDecimal(8)}, observed ratio of errors ${c.ratio.toFixed(6)}`);

// Newton with fractions: no rounding, but the denominators double in length.
for (const row of newton("x^2 - 2", "1", { exact: true, steps: 5 }).iterations) PRINT(`x${row.n} = ${row.x}   (${row.denominatorDigits} digits, error ${row.error.toExponential(1)})`);

// A double root: Newton drops to order 1.
newton("(x - 1)^2*(x + 2)", 2, { steps: 20 }).order.toFixed(2);
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/descent.html

Numerical methods

## Gradient descent

Gradient descent walks downhill: from a point x it steps against the gradient, x←x−t∇f(x). `gradientDescent` runs the method and keeps its table. When f is built from +, −, ×, ÷ and integer powers, every iterate, value, gradient and step is an exact fraction, so the table is what the method does with no rounding at all; otherwise it runs in floating point. The result is labelled `simulated`: it shows the method from one start and proves nothing about a minimum. For a certified minimum use [extrema](https://ratmath.com/analytic/zeros.html) on one variable or [lagrange](https://ratmath.com/analytic/multipliers.html) with constraints.

```js
const r = gradientDescent("x^2 + 4*y^2", ["1", "1"], { step: "1/10", steps: 2 });
r.iterations.map((row) => row.x);   // [[1, 1], [4/5, 1/5], [16/25, 1/25]]
r.simulated;                          // true
```

### Choosing the step

- Fixed (method: "fixed", step = 1/10 by default). The same t every time. For f=x2+4y2 a step above 1/4 makes the y coordinate grow: the step must be below 2/L where L is the largest curvature.

- Backtracking ("backtracking"). Start at step (default 1) and halve until the Armijo condition f(x−tg)≤f(x)−ct∣g∣2 holds, with c = armijo (default 1/2). Each step is then guaranteed to decrease f by a fixed fraction of what the slope promised.

- Exact line search ("exact"), for a quadratic f=21​xTHx+bTx+c. Along x−tg the value is a parabola in t, minimised at

t∗=gTHggTg​.
Successive gradients are then perpendicular, which is why the path zigzags when the level sets are long ellipses. With exact fractions this is visible exactly: the dot product of consecutive gradients is 0, not a small number.

| call | returns |

| gradientDescent(f, start, { variables, method = "fixed", step, steps = 10, armijo = "1/2" }) | { simulated: true, method, variables, iterations: [{ n, x, fx, gradient, step }], final, value, exact } |

### Try it

```js
// Three ways to choose the step on f = x^2 + 4y^2 from (1, 1), all in exact fractions.
for (const method of ["fixed", "backtracking", "exact"]) {
  const r = gradientDescent("x^2 + 4*y^2", ["1", "1"], { method, step: method === "fixed" ? "1/10" : undefined, steps: 4 });
  PRINT(method.padEnd(12), r.iterations.map((row) => `(${row.x.join(", ")})`).join(" → "));
}

// With the exact line search, consecutive gradients are exactly perpendicular.
const e = gradientDescent("x^2 + 4*y^2 + x*y", ["2", "1"], { method: "exact", steps: 3 });
const g = e.iterations.map((row) => row.gradient);
PRINT("g0·g1 =", g[0][0].multiply(g[1][0]).add(g[0][1].multiply(g[1][1])), "  g1·g2 =", g[1][0].multiply(g[2][0]).add(g[1][1].multiply(g[2][1])));

// Too large a fixed step diverges.
PRINT("step 3/10:", gradientDescent("x^2 + 4*y^2", ["1", "1"], { step: "3/10", steps: 4 }).iterations.map((row) => row.x[1]).join(", "));

// A non-polynomial objective runs in floating point.
gradientDescent("exp(x) + x^2", ["1"], { method: "backtracking", steps: 6 }).final
```

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/interpolation.html

Numerical methods

## Interpolation and approximation

The polynomial through a set of points, in Newton's and Lagrange's forms with exact divided differences; the error formula beside the true error; Chebyshev nodes and the Runge phenomenon; natural cubic splines and least-squares polynomials, all with exact rational coefficients.

```js
const p = interpolate([[0, 1], [1, 3], [2, 2]]);
p.polynomial;            // "-3/2*x^2 + 7/2*x + 1"
p.newton;                // "1 + 2*x - 3/2*x*(x - 1)"
p.dividedDifferences;    // [[1, 3, 2], [2, -1], [-3/2]]   exact
p.at("1/2");             // 19/8

const q = interpolate("sin(x)", { nodes: equallySpaced(0, 1, 4) });
q.maxError([0, 1]);      // { value, attained, at, textbook }
```

### Divided differences

Through n+1 points with distinct xi​ there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n. Newton's form builds it one node at a time:

p(x)=f[x0​]+f[x0​,x1​](x−x0​)+f[x0​,x1​,x2​](x−x0​)(x−x1​)+…,f[xi​,…,xi+k​]=xi+k​−xi​f[xi+1​,…,xi+k​]−f[xi​,…,xi+k−1​]​.
The table of divided differences is computed in exact rational arithmetic, so for data given as rationals the polynomial is the true one, with no rounding. Lagrange's form writes the same polynomial as ∑yi​ℓi​(x), where ℓi​ is 1 at xi​ and 0 at the other nodes.

### The error formula

If f has n+1 continuous derivatives, then for each x there is a ξ with

f(x)−p(x)=(n+1)!f(n+1)(ξ)​i=0∏n​(x−xi​).
`maxError` reports the true maximum of ∣f−p∣ on an interval, bracketed between a value attained and a proven upper bound, and beside it the bound the formula gives, max∣f(n+1)∣/(n+1)!⋅max∣∏(x−xi​)∣, with both maxima enclosed.

### Runge's example and Chebyshev nodes

More nodes need not mean a better fit. For f(x)=1/(1+25x2) on [−1,1] with equally spaced nodes the error near the ends grows without bound as the degree rises. The product ∏(x−xi​) is the part of the error formula that the choice of nodes controls, and it is smallest in maximum when the nodes are the Chebyshev points

xi​=cos2n(2i+1)π​,i=0,…,n−1,
which crowd towards the ends. `chebyshevNodes(a, b, n)` returns them rounded to nearby rationals.

### Splines and least squares

A natural cubic spline is a cubic on each interval between nodes, with two continuous derivatives across the nodes and zero second derivative at the two ends. The second derivatives at the nodes solve a tridiagonal system, here exactly. A least-squares polynomial of degree d minimises ∑(p(xi​)−yi​)2; its coefficients solve the normal equations ATAc=ATy, again exactly, and the residual is returned as an exact rational.

| call | returns |

| interpolate(points) or interpolate(f, { nodes }) | { nodes, values, dividedDifferences, newton, lagrange, polynomial, coefficients, at(x), error(x), maxError([a, b]) } |

| equallySpaced(a, b, n), chebyshevNodes(a, b, n) | arrays of Rationals |

| spline(points) | { pieces: [{ from, to, coefficients, polynomial }], moments, at(x) } |

| leastSquares(points, degree = 1) | { coefficients, polynomial, residual, at(x) } |

### Try it

```js
// The table of divided differences for four values of 1/x.
const p = interpolate("1/x", { nodes: [1, 2, 3, 4] });
p.dividedDifferences.forEach((row, k) => PRINT(`order ${k}:`, row.map(String).join("   ")));
PRINT("Newton form:", p.newton);
PRINT("expanded:   ", p.polynomial);
const e = p.maxError([1, 4]);
PRINT(`max |1/x - p| on [1, 4]: between ${e.attained.toDecimal(6)} and ${e.value.toDecimal(6)}; the error formula promises at most ${e.textbook.toDecimal(6)}`);

// Runge's example: equally spaced nodes against Chebyshev nodes.
const f = "1/(1 + 25*x^2)";
for (const n of [5, 9]) {
  const equal = interpolate(f, { nodes: equallySpaced(-1, 1, n) }).maxError([-1, 1], { tolerance: 0.05 });
  const cheb = interpolate(f, { nodes: chebyshevNodes(-1, 1, n) }).maxError([-1, 1], { tolerance: 0.05 });
  PRINT(`${n} nodes: equally spaced max error ${equal.value.toDecimal(4)}, Chebyshev ${cheb.value.toDecimal(4)}`);
}

// A natural spline and a least-squares line through the same points.
const pts = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [2, 0], [3, 1]];
for (const piece of spline(pts).pieces) PRINT(`spline on [${piece.from}, ${piece.to}]: ${piece.polynomial}`);
const line = leastSquares(pts, 1);
`least-squares line ${line.polynomial}, sum of squares ${line.residual}`;
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/quadraturerules.html

Numerical methods

## Differences and quadrature rules

The classical formulas for derivatives and integrals, with the true error of each beside the textbook estimate: difference quotients and the step size at which rounding takes over, Richardson extrapolation, the composite midpoint, trapezoid and Simpson rules, Romberg's table, and Gauss-Legendre rules with certified nodes and weights.

```js
const d = differences("exp(x)", 1, { kind: "central" });
d.rows;    // [{ h, value, error, truncation }, …]  for h = 1e-1 … 1e-12
d.best;    // the h with the smallest true error

quadratureRule("exp(x)", [0, 1], { rule: "simpson", n: 4 });
// { value, exact, error, bound, order: 4 }

gaussLegendre(3);   // { polynomial: "5/2*x^3 - 3/2*x", nodes, weights }  enclosures
```

### Difference quotients

| kind | formula | truncation error |

| forward | hf(x+h)−f(x)​ | 21​f′′(x)h |

| central | 2hf(x+h)−f(x−h)​ | 61​f(3)(x)h2 |

| second | h2f(x+h)−2f(x)+f(x−h)​ | 121​f(4)(x)h2 |

The truncation error shrinks with h. The rounding error grows: the numerator is a difference of nearly equal numbers, accurate to about ε∣f∣ with ε≈10−16, and dividing by h makes that ε∣f∣/h. The total is smallest near h≈ε​ for the forward difference and h≈ε1/3 for the central one. `differences` evaluates the quotient in doubles for a range of h and reports the true error of each against the certified derivative, so the turn is visible in the table, with the predicted truncation term beside it.

### Richardson extrapolation

The central difference has an error expansion in even powers, D(h)=f′(x)+c2​h2+c4​h4+…. Then (4D(h/2)−D(h))/3 cancels the h2 term, and repeating the idea cancels h4, h6, and so on. `richardson` builds the triangular table; `romberg` does the same for the trapezoid rule, whose error has the same kind of expansion (Euler-Maclaurin).

### Composite rules

| rule | on each panel of width h | error bound |

| midpoint | hf(mid) | 24(b−a)h2​max∣f′′∣ |

| trapezoid | 2h​(f(left)+f(right)) | 12(b−a)h2​max∣f′′∣ |

| Simpson | 6h​(f(left)+4f(mid)+f(right)) | 2880(b−a)h4​max∣f(4)∣ |

`quadratureRule` evaluates the rule with certified arithmetic, so `error` is the error of the method alone, with no rounding mixed in. `exact` is the certified integral and `bound` the textbook bound with the maximum of the derivative enclosed. The true error is always inside the bound, and usually well inside.

### Darboux sums

The lower and upper Darboux sums of a partition use the inf and the sup of f on each piece, L=∑mi​Δxi​ and U=∑Mi​Δxi​, and every integral lies between them. `darboux(f, partition)` takes a list of points or `{ interval, n }`. On a piece where f′ is proven to have one sign, f is monotone and its inf and sup are its end values, so for a polynomial or rational function the sums are exact fractions: for x2 on [0,1] with four pieces, L=327​ and U=3215​. Where monotonicity is not proven, the inf and sup come from the end values and the certified critical points inside, the sums are intervals that contain the true sums, and `exact` is false.

### Gauss rules

With n points chosen freely, a rule can be exact for all polynomials of degree below 2n. The points are the roots of the Legendre polynomial Pn​, and the weights are wi​=2/((1−xi2​)Pn′​(xi​)2). `gaussLegendre(n)` builds Pn​ with exact coefficients, isolates its roots with proof, and returns nodes and weights as enclosures to 25 digits.

| call | returns |

| differences(f, x, { kind = "central", steps }) | { exact, order, rows: [{ h, value, error, truncation }], best } |

| richardson(f, x, { h = 0.5, levels = 5 }) | { table, errors, exact } |

| quadratureRule(f, [a, b], { rule, n }) | { value, exact, error, bound, order, h } |

| darboux(f, points) or darboux(f, { interval: [a, b], n }) | { lower, upper, exact, pieces: [{ from, to, monotone, inf, sup }], integral }; Rationals when exact, else RationalIntervals |

| romberg(f, [a, b], { levels = 5 }) | { table, errors, exact } |

| gaussLegendre(n), legendre(n) | { polynomial, nodes, weights }; coefficients of Pₙ |

| gaussRule(f, [a, b], n = 3) | { value, exact, error, nodes, weights } |

### Try it

```js
// The derivative of exp at 1 by central differences: the error falls like h², then rounding wins.
const d = differences("exp(x)", 1, { kind: "central" });
for (const r of d.rows) PRINT(`h = ${r.h.toExponential(0)}   error ${r.error.toExponential(2)}   truncation term ${r.truncation.toExponential(2)}`);
PRINT("best h:", d.best.h, " Richardson from h = 1/2, five levels: error", richardson("exp(x)", 1).errors.at(-1).at(-1).toExponential(1));

// Rules on the integral of exp over [0, 1]: true error against the textbook bound.
for (const rule of ["midpoint", "trapezoid", "simpson"]) {
  for (const n of [4, 8]) {
    const q = quadratureRule("exp(x)", [0, 1], { rule, n });
    PRINT(`${rule.padEnd(9)} n = ${n}: error ${q.error.low.toNumber().toExponential(3)}   bound ${q.bound.toNumber().toExponential(3)}`);
  }
}

// Darboux sums of x^2 on [0, 1] squeeze 1/3; sin on [0, 3] gets enclosures.
for (const n of [4, 16, 64]) {
  const d = darboux("x^2", { interval: [0, 1], n });
  PRINT(`n = ${n}: ${d.lower} ≤ 1/3 ≤ ${d.upper}`);
}
const ds = darboux("sin(x)", { interval: [0, 3], n: 3 });
PRINT("sin on [0, 3]:", ds.pieces.map((p) => p.monotone ?? "turns").join(", "), " lower", ds.lower.low.toDecimal(6), " upper", ds.upper.high.toDecimal(6));

// Three Gauss points beat eight Simpson panels.
const g = gaussRule("exp(x)", [0, 1], 3);
PRINT("Gauss, 3 points: error", g.error.low.toNumber().toExponential(3));
PRINT("nodes:", gaussLegendre(3).nodes.map((x) => x.low.toDecimal(15)).join(", "));
romberg("exp(x)", [0, 1], { levels: 4 }).errors.map((row) => row.map((e) => e.toExponential(1)).join("  "));
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/analytic/odemethods.html

Numerical methods

## Euler to Runge-Kutta

The one-step methods for y′=f(t,y) and a two-step method, run in doubles with their table of steps. The [validated solver](https://ratmath.com/analytic/odes.html) supplies the true solution at every step, so the global error is in the table, and halving the step shows each method's order.

```js
const r = odeMethod("y - t^2 + 1", { y0: "1/2", until: 2, steps: 10, method: "rk4" });
r.steps;        // [{ n, t, y, exact, error }, …]
r.finalError;   // the true error at t = 2

stepSizeStudy("y - t^2 + 1", { y0: "1/2", until: 2, method: "euler" }).rows;
// [{ steps, h, error, ratio, observedOrder }, …]

stability("rk4").interval;   // [-2.785…, 0]
```

### The methods

| method | step from (t,y) with size h | order |

| euler | y+hf(t,y) | 1 |

| heun | y+2h​(k1​+f(t+h, y+hk1​)), k1​=f(t,y) | 2 |

| midpoint | y+hf(t+2h​, y+2h​k1​) | 2 |

| rk4 | y+6h​(k1​+2k2​+2k3​+k4​), the classical four stages | 4 |

| ab2 | y+2h​(3fn​−fn−1​), Adams-Bashforth, started with one Heun step | 2 |

### Local and global error

A method of order p makes an error of size hp+1 in one step (the local error). Over the 1/h steps needed to cross a fixed interval these add up, and the global error at the end is of size hp. So halving h divides the final error by about 2p: by 2 for Euler, by 16 for the classical Runge-Kutta method. `stepSizeStudy` runs the same problem with several step counts and reports the ratio of successive errors and the order it implies.

The errors are true ones: at each step the method's double is compared with the validated enclosure of y(tn​), and `error` is the largest possible distance between them.

### Stability

On the test equation y′=λy each of these methods multiplies y by a polynomial R(hλ) per step: 1+z for Euler, 1+z+21​z2 for the second-order methods, and the degree-4 Taylor polynomial of ez for rk4. The true solution decays when λ; the numerical one decays only when ∣R(hλ)∣. For real negative z that is an interval, (−2,0) for Euler and (−2.785…,0) for rk4, with the left end enclosed here as a root of R(z)=1. A step size outside it makes the computed solution grow although the true one dies away: the reason stiff equations force small steps on explicit methods.

| call | returns |

| odeMethod(f, { y0, t0 = 0, until, steps = 10, method }) | { method, order, h, steps: [{ n, t, y, exact, error }], finalError } |

| stepSizeStudy(f, { …, counts }) | { rows: [{ steps, h, error, ratio, observedOrder }] } |

| stability(method) | { polynomial, interval, largestStep(lambda) } |

### Try it

```js
// y' = y - t^2 + 1, y(0) = 1/2 on [0, 2]: five methods, ten steps each.
const problem = { y0: "1/2", until: 2, steps: 10 };
for (const method of ["euler", "heun", "midpoint", "ab2", "rk4"]) {
  const r = odeMethod("y - t^2 + 1", { ...problem, method });
  PRINT(`${method.padEnd(8)} y(2) = ${r.steps.at(-1).y.toFixed(10)}   true error ${r.finalError.toExponential(3)}`);
}
PRINT("validated y(2):", odeMethod("y - t^2 + 1", { ...problem }).steps.at(-1).exact.low.toDecimal(12));

// Halving the step: the error ratio shows the order.
for (const method of ["euler", "heun", "rk4"]) {
  const s = stepSizeStudy("y - t^2 + 1", { y0: "1/2", until: 2, method, counts: [10, 20, 40, 80] });
  PRINT(`${method.padEnd(6)} observed orders: ${s.rows.slice(1).map((r) => r.observedOrder.toFixed(3)).join(", ")}`);
}

// A stiff problem: y' = -50(y - cos t). Euler is stable only for h < 2/50.
for (const steps of [20, 30, 100]) {
  const r = odeMethod("-50*(y - cos(t))", { y0: 0, until: 1, steps, method: "euler" });
  PRINT(`Euler with h = ${r.h}: error at t = 1 is ${r.finalError.toExponential(2)}`);
}
`largest stable Euler step for λ = -50: ${stability("euler").largestStep(-50).low}; for rk4: ${stability("rk4").largestStep(-50).low.toDecimal(5)}`;
```
